title: For First Nations, Trump’s lake renaming is much ado about Niiganii-gichigami
content:
Lake Ontario is Niiganii-gichigami in the Anishinaabemowin language. Elders tell me the lake was always known as this.
But what, exactly, is in a name?
For First Nations people, I know that regardless of which community you are from, names have meaning. They can provide information, and signify respect. So when an American President renames a body of water on an angry whim by writing “Lake America” over “Lake Ontario” on a map with a marker, it means nothing to us – those who have lived here since before all these lines were drawn and borders created.
Mr. Trump loves to recolonize. He did it to the Gulf of Mexico in January, 2025, when he renamed it the Gulf of America. He also changed the name of the Alaskan mountain Denali, which had been reverted to that traditional Koyukon Athabascan name under Barack Obama, to Mount McKinley. But the Anishinaabeg have lived in and around the Great Lakes since well before Canada or America was a country. In Anishinaabemowin, the “Great Lakes” are Nayaano-nibiimaang gichigamiin: the five freshwater seas. Niiganii-gichigami, our name for Lake Ontario, translates to “the leading lake.” “Ontario,” meanwhile, comes from either Wendat or the Haudenosaunee word “kanadario,” referring to beautiful or sparkling water; the Haudenosaunee, the people of the long house, also live here, and the Wendat were an Iroquoian speaking nation.
Rift with Canada shows potential to become a pressing U.S. election issue
My friend, Dehaeho:węhs Amos Key Jr., is a Faith Keeper from Six Nations of the Grand River in Ohsweken. When I asked him what Ontario means, he said: “When you study the etymology of our Haudenosaunee languages, and you add the suffix ‘ri:io to a word or phrase, it gives it the meaning of something being very precious, coveted and gifted from Shögwayadisöh, our Creator.” The French picked it up and the name has been in use since 1641, noted Prime Minister Mark Carney, who schooled the U.S. leader about the origins of the name on X. “The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” he said. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
The Prime Minister was right to brush off Mr. Trump’s silly stunt – especially during an escalating trade war. The fact that Mr. Trump was focused on such colonizing tactics shows you where his head is at and what his ambitions are.
But this is what we know: An American President can never take away the name of a lake that was never his in the first place. Water can’t be owned. Water is alive. It has spirit. It ebbs and flows and it fills our bodies. Water gives us life and it can take it away. Renaming our beautiful, glimmering and wide Niiganii-gichigami “Lake America” means nothing to any of us living here in Canada.
In a trade war, can you shop your way to patriotism?
Mr. Trump’s childlike act has only mobilized Canadians, and brought us closer together. Suddenly, those who live here are getting a taste of the threat of colonization. Indigenous people have experienced this before, more than 150 years ago. We know how this playbook goes. But this time, those who colonized our ancestors are being threatened alongside us.
This is a tiresome fight, and Indigenous peoples have seen it all before. We are so done with those that come from foreign lands to take our water, our critical minerals, our sense of self. They will not tell us who we are. It makes sense that it was Manitoba’s Anishinaabe Premier, Wab Kinew, who pushed back when the Prime Minister asked the provinces to return American alcohol to liquor-store shelves ahead of the since-scuttled deal. “Very wise people have said you can’t get a good deal with a bad person,” the Premier said. We still have agency, Mr. Kinew said, so we don’t have to give in to a bully and make a deal that leads us down the wrong path, even if it hurts: “I think we should fight.”
Canadians now have a choice. They can look inward. Buy food grown on this land. Change habits. Learn and embrace true history, not deny it. Be proud of the Indigenous peoples who have taken care of the waters, the Earth, the animals. Recognize our collective history by, among other things, supporting Orange Shirt Day on Sept. 30. And we can act like we say we are: Canadians who say “Ontario” and “Niiganii-gichigami,” because the whims of an American politician mean nothing to those of us with long memories.

title: Alfonso Durazo rompe récord educativo en Sonora con más de 736 mil becas entregadas
content:
Sonora registra una inversión y cobertura sin precedentes en apoyo a estudiantes. Durante los cinco años de la administración del gobernador Alfonso Durazo Montaño se han entregado más de 736 mil becas, en una entidad que cuenta con alrededor de 805 mil estudiantes.
La cifra permite dimensionar el alcance de la estrategia: el número de becas entregadas equivale a más de nueve apoyos por cada 10 estudiantes que integran la comunidad estudiantil sonorense.
Para alcanzar esta cobertura, el Gobierno de Sonora ha destinado más de 3 mil 700 millones de pesos exclusivamente a becas, una inversión que supera por más del doble lo ejercido durante los tres sexenios anteriores juntos, es decir, los 18 años previos.
Por primera vez en la entidad, los apoyos abarcan todos los niveles educativos, desde educación básica hasta nivel superior, a través de Becas Sonora de Oportunidades, el programa de becas más grande en la historia del estado.
La estrategia impulsada por Durazo no se limita al apoyo económico. En cinco años se han entregado 2 millones 230 mil paquetes de uniformes escolares gratuitos, reduciendo gastos para las familias y garantizando mejores condiciones para que niñas, niños y jóvenes continúen sus estudios.
Para el ciclo escolar actual, con el apoyo del Gobierno de México, Sonora fue el primer estado del país en la distribución de más de 3 millones de libros de texto gratuitos, mientras que 94 mil 800 estudiantes son beneficiarios de desayunos escolares, como parte de una política que busca atender las condiciones que inciden directamente en la permanencia y el aprendizaje.
En infraestructura, el Gobierno de Sonora ha invertido 3 mil 364 millones de pesos en construcción, rehabilitación y mejoramiento de planteles educativos, con obras para dignificar los espacios donde se forman las nuevas generaciones.
Los resultados colocan a la educación como uno de los principales ejes de la administración estatal: más de 736 mil becas entregadas, 2 millones 230 mil paquetes de uniformes, más de 3 millones de libros de texto gratuitos en el presente ciclo, alimentación para cerca de 195 mil estudiantes y más de 3 mil 300 millones de pesos destinados a infraestructura educativa.
Para el gobernador Alfonso Durazo, la apuesta es que el origen o la condición económica de una familia no determinen hasta dónde puede llegar un estudiante.
En Sonora, la diferencia frente al pasado se refleja en la inversión: en solo cinco años se han destinado a becas más del doble de recursos que en los 18 años anteriores, convirtiendo a la educación en una de las principales herramientas para ampliar oportunidades y transformar el futuro de una generación.

title: Έξι φορές λιγότεροι νεκροί όπου υπάρχει έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση
content:
Μερικά λεπτά ή λίγες ώρες προειδοποίησης μπορούν να κάνουν τη διαφορά ανάμεσα στη ζωή και τον θάνατο όταν πλησιάζει μια πλημμύρα, ένας κυκλώνας ή ένα άλλο ακραίο φυσικό φαινόμενο. Και πλέον υπάρχουν στοιχεία που δείχνουν πόσο μεγάλη μπορεί να είναι αυτή η διαφορά.
Στις χώρες που διαθέτουν ολοκληρωμένα συστήματα έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης για πολλαπλούς κινδύνους, η θνησιμότητα από καταστροφές είναι έξι φορές χαμηλότερη σε σύγκριση με τις χώρες που δεν διαθέτουν αντίστοιχους μηχανισμούς, σύμφωνα με νέα έκθεση του ΟΗΕ.
Τα στοιχεία παρουσιάστηκαν ενώ οι παγκόσμιοι ηγέτες βρίσκονται στη Νέα Υόρκη για τη Σύνοδο του ΟΗΕ για το Κλίμα και καταγράφουν την πρόοδο της πρωτοβουλίας Early Warnings for All – Έγκαιρη Προειδοποίηση για Όλους, η οποία ξεκίνησε το 2022.
Ο στόχος είναι εξαιρετικά φιλόδοξος: μέχρι το τέλος του 2027 κάθε άνθρωπος στον πλανήτη να προστατεύεται από κάποιο αποτελεσματικό σύστημα έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης.
Από 56 σε 136 χώρες
Η πρόοδος των τελευταίων ετών είναι σημαντική. Σήμερα 136 χώρες διαθέτουν δυνατότητες έγκαιρης προειδοποίησης για πολλαπλούς κινδύνους, αριθμός αυξημένος κατά 143% σε σχέση με το 2015.
Παράλληλα, περισσότερες από 160 χώρες λαμβάνουν άμεση υποστήριξη για να ενισχύσουν τα συστήματά τους.
Μόνο την περίοδο 2022-2025 κινητοποιήθηκαν περίπου 2 δισ. δολάρια, με στόχο τη βελτίωση της προετοιμασίας, την προστασία ευάλωτων πληθυσμών και την ενίσχυση της δυνατότητας των κρατών να προβλέπουν και να αντιμετωπίζουν έγκαιρα τις καταστροφές.
Τα συστήματα αυτά δεν περιορίζονται σε μια εφαρμογή στο κινητό ή σε μια σειρήνα συναγερμού. Απαιτούν μετεωρολογικά και υδρολογικά δεδομένα, δίκτυα παρατήρησης, αξιόπιστες προβλέψεις, τηλεπικοινωνιακές υποδομές και κυρίως έναν μηχανισμό που μετατρέπει την επιστημονική πληροφορία σε συγκεκριμένη προειδοποίηση προς τον πολίτη.
Γιατί μια ακριβής πρόγνωση που δεν φτάνει εγκαίρως σε όσους κινδυνεύουν έχει ελάχιστη πρακτική αξία.
Όταν η προειδοποίηση έρχεται πριν από την καταστροφή
Χαρακτηριστικό παράδειγμα αποτελεί η Κολομβία. Τον Ιούνιο του 2026, ο Ερυθρός Σταυρός της χώρας ενεργοποίησε πρωτόκολλο έγκαιρης δράσης για την ξηρασία, μόλις εμφανίστηκαν οι πρώτες ενδείξεις του Ελ Νίνιο και πριν οι συνθήκες φτάσουν σε κρίσιμο επίπεδο.
Αυτή είναι η φιλοσοφία του νέου μοντέλου: οι αρχές να μην περιμένουν να συμβεί η καταστροφή για να κινητοποιηθούν, αλλά να δρουν όταν υπάρχουν πλέον επαρκείς ενδείξεις ότι αυτή πλησιάζει.
Το 2025, τέτοιες προληπτικές δράσεις έφτασαν σε 9,6 εκατομμύρια ανθρώπους σε 54 χώρες, μέσα από 146 ενεργοποιήσεις προγραμμάτων που υποστηρίχθηκαν με σχεδόν 120 εκατ. δολάρια.
Το τραγικό παράδειγμα του Νεπάλ
Η άλλη πλευρά του προβλήματος φαίνεται όταν το σύστημα δεν υπάρχει ή δεν λειτουργεί.
Κατά τις καταστροφικές παγετωνικές πλημμύρες του Αυγούστου στο Νεπάλ, οι κοινότητες που βρίσκονταν κατάντη έλαβαν ελάχιστη ή καθόλου έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση. Ο χρόνος για εκκένωση ήταν σχεδόν ανύπαρκτος.
Ο απολογισμός ήταν δραματικός: περισσότεροι από 1.000 νεκροί, χιλιάδες αγνοούμενοι και πάνω από 10.000 εκτοπισμένοι, μαζί με τεράστιες καταστροφές σε κατοικίες και κρίσιμες υποδομές.
Η περίπτωση δείχνει γιατί η έγκαιρη προειδοποίηση δεν αποτελεί απλώς ένα ακόμη εργαλείο πολιτικής προστασίας, αλλά βασική υποδομή μιας χώρας που βρίσκεται αντιμέτωπη με ολοένα συχνότερα και εντονότερα ακραία φαινόμενα.
Τα μεγαλύτερα κενά στους πιο ευάλωτους
Το παράδοξο είναι ότι οι μεγαλύτερες ελλείψεις εντοπίζονται ακριβώς στις χώρες που είναι περισσότερο εκτεθειμένες.
Οι λιγότερο ανεπτυγμένες χώρες, τα μικρά αναπτυσσόμενα νησιωτικά κράτη και οι περιοχές που πλήττονται από συγκρούσεις εξακολουθούν να παρουσιάζουν σοβαρά κενά.
Αυτά αφορούν την καταγραφή και κατανόηση των κινδύνων, τις υποδομές παρατήρησης και πρόγνωσης, τις τηλεπικοινωνίες, την επιχειρησιακή ικανότητα των αρχών και την προετοιμασία των ίδιων των κοινωνιών.
Περίπου 50 χώρες συμμετέχουν πλέον ενεργά στην εφαρμογή της πρωτοβουλίας του ΟΗΕ, ενώ έχουν δημιουργηθεί 31 εθνικοί οδικοί χάρτες.
Το μήνυμα του Αντόνιο Γκουτέρες είναι ότι η πρόοδος δεν αρκεί. Εκατομμύρια άνθρωποι εξακολουθούν να μένουν απροστάτευτοι.
Σε έναν πλανήτη όπου οι ακραίες θερμοκρασίες, οι πλημμύρες, οι ξηρασίες και οι πυρκαγιές εντείνονται, η προσαρμογή στην κλιματική κρίση δεν αφορά μόνο μεγάλα έργα και δισεκατομμύρια επενδύσεων.
Μερικές φορές αρχίζει από κάτι πολύ πιο απλό: να γνωρίζει κάποιος εγκαίρως ότι ο κίνδυνος έρχεται.

title: How New Zealand’s invisible Indian pioneers became a vital part of national identity
content:
The Indian community's long history in New Zealand is full of rich stories of resilience, adaption and eventual triumph as the migrants evolved from invisible pioneers to become a vital part of the country's national identity
The Indian Association Manukau highlighted some of these incredible stories in a theatrical production in Auckland on Saturday that was organised to celebrate the centenary of the New Zealand Indian Central Association, which was founded in 1926 to counter increasing racism.
The two-hour-long show was based on a 2007 book by historian Jacqueline Leckie titled Indian Settlers: The Story of a New Zealand South Asian Community.
Leckie expanded on her earlier work by publishing Invisible: New Zealand's History of Excluding Kiwi Indians in 2021 and Wellington's Indian Story: Beyond a Century Four Years Later.
Divided into several acts, the theatre production touched on the story of brothers Bir and Phuman (Phomen) Singh Gill, who, according to a 1988 book by historian W.H. McLeod titled Punjabis in New Zealand: A History of Punjabi Migration 1890-1940, likely arrived in New Zealand around 1890.
While the Gill brothers were among the early Punjabi settlers, the honour of arguably being the first Gujarati to arrive in New Zealand belongs to Keshaw Daji, who historians believe relocated here in 1902.
The weekend production also featured Edward Peters, who, according to a book by historians Sekhar Bandyopadhyay and Jane Buckingham titled Indians and the Antipodes, was the first Indian to achieve fame in New Zealand.
"[He] was an Anglo-Indian from [the Indian state of] Goa who arrived in 1853, having previously worked at the California gold fields," the authors wrote.
"Edward Peter, later known as 'Black Peter', was a farm labourer and gold prospector."
A memorial to the 19th-century prospector, calling him Edward Peters, was unveiled near Milton in Central Otago in 2009.
The third act of the production described the early Indian community's foray into market gardening in South Auckland, mainly Otahuhu and Pukekohe.
The production paid homage to the fight for independence from colonial rule in South Asia, featuring a depiction of the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
The most moving part of the show was when actors on stage described the discrimination that early Indians faced in New Zealand, and how the community fought back united under one voice.
Battling discrimination
The early Indian pioneers recognised the importance of working together as a collective, which led to the formation of the Auckland Indian Association in 1920 - the first Indian community organisation in New Zealand.
This was followed by the establishment of the Wellington Indian Association in 1925 and the Country Section New Zealand Indian Association in 1926.
Later that year, these three organisations joined forces to create a national body called the New Zealand Indian Central Association after racism against Indians became more entrenched in the 1920s with the formation of the White New Zealand League.
The Immigration Restriction Amendment Act 1920, which initiated agitation against Asian immigration, didn't help either.
The newly formed Indian associations collectively fought discrimination against the community through lawful means and defended the rightful place of Indians as British subjects in New Zealand.
However, discrimination against Indians continued for decades, as documented by Leckie in her books.
Some such instances were illustrated at the theatrical production on Saturday, including re-enactments of Indians being excluded from whites-only spaces in Pukekohe.
"Barbers refused to cut the hair of Chinese, Māori or Indians," Leckie wrote in Invisible: New Zealand's History of Excluding Kiwi Indians.
"These groups were also banned from the better-quality dress circle within a Pukekohe cinema."
There were also differences in treatment between white- and dark-skinned people at the Tepid Baths in central Auckland during that time.
Things improved after New Zealand introduced progressive reform to its immigration policy in 1958 that opened the gates to immigration.
The theatre production noted how these reforms allowed New Zealand-born Indian women to bring in husbands from other countries, including India.
Previously the act permitted only Indian men born here to bring in wives and children who were minors.
Universal praise
Former Governor-General Sir Anand Satyanand - arguably the most well-known Kiwi-Indian in the room - called the production "a wonderful expression of the contribution of the Indian community in New Zealand".
"So many people contributed to make it happen ... the cast was so wonderful," he said, acknowledging the 80-plus people - all amateur actors - who have been practising for months to deliver their lines on stage.
Special praise was reserved for former teacher and production director Godrej Engineer.
Labour list MP of Indian-origin Priyanca Radhakrishnan was moved by the stories of migrant Indian women "who are often overlooked in such discussions".
Radhakrishnan was inspired by the way in which the Indian community in New Zealand united to fight against oppression.
Leckie, who attended as a special guest, was impressed to see "history translated into a creative form".
Veer Khar, president of the New Zealand Indian Central Association, praised the early pioneers who collectively fought for respect.
"While there is still some work to be done, organisations such as NZICA have worked tirelessly to ensure level playing fields for Indians in New Zealand," Khar said.
Earlier in the year, Khar called on the government to acknowledge the discrimination the Indian community had faced throughout the country's history.
"As we mark an important milestone [100 years of NZICA] this year, the Indian community is rallying for [an] acknowledgement of [the] historical racism it has faced in the country - along the lines of the Chinese poll tax apology and Dawn Raids apology delivered to the Pacific communities in the past," Khar said in March.
Other initiatives
The New Zealand Indian Central Association also released a documentary this week titled Lotus in the Long White Cloud, produced and directed by Roy Kaunds and Ajay Vasisht.
The duo took almost six months researching and shooting the film, describing it as "a big eye-opener".
The documentary documents instances of Indians being called "dirty", "curry munchers" and refused jobs because of their skin colour.
"[This is] a journey of how our previous generations overcame adversity and became achievers in a foreign land," Kaunds had told RNZ earlier.
In mid-2025, another documentary titled Punjab to Aotearoa was released that aimed to trace the history of Indian migration to New Zealand over the past 100 years.
Presented by Harjot Singh, the 48-minute documentary was directed by Gagan Sandhu.
It was co-produced by Parminder Singh, host at Punjabi radio station Radio Spice, and Navtej Randhawa, a trustee at NZ Punjabi Multimedia Trust, which backed the documentary.
"[This is] the first part of a series we will be producing [in future], ... documenting the proud history of Indian migration to Aotearoa New Zealand, especially from the villages of Punjab," Randhawa told RNZ then.
Randhawa is great-grandson of Inder Singh Randhawa, one of the early Indian migrants to New Zealand and a founding member of pioneering Indian associations including the Country Section New Zealand Indian Association and New Zealand Indian Central Association.
"This documentary is a preservation of our legacy, a gift for generations to come," Randhawa said.
In November 2024, the Indian community rallied around an exhibition titled Asha ka Darwaza (Doorways of Hope), which was on display at Auckland's Mahatma Gandhi Centre for weeks and gave visitors a rare opportunity to trace the rich history of New Zealand's Indian community.
Organised by the Auckland Indian Association, the exhibition in Eden Terrace showcased artifacts, photographs and displays that honoured the cultural heritage and resilient spirit of a community that first started migrating to New Zealand in the late 18th century.
Meanwhile as the show ended on Saturday, Khar promised the crew that more work lay ahead.
"Get ready for Wellington," he said, indicating plans to showcase the theatrical production in the capital soon.

title: Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
content:
Preserving Ernie Barnes’s Legacy in Paint Tubes
The late artist and athlete who rendered joyous scenes of Black life, dance, and motion is the subject of renewed institutional attention as his daughter, Erin Barnes, works to conserve his studio practice.
When artist Ernie Barnes died in 2009, his daughter Erin was left to sort through the vestiges of materials the Los Angeles-based painter and professional football player had accumulated over his decades-long art practice.
There were canvases, sure, but also paint tubes, brushes, and containers Barnes kept in the garage that he used as his studio to create vibrant, kinetic scenes of Black church gatherings, football games, and nightlife during the Jim Crow era, including his iconic work “The Sugar Shack” (1976), making him one of Southern California’s most beloved artists.
For years, Barnes stored her father’s partially squeezed containers of Liquitex, Grumbacher, and Winsor & Newton acrylic paint and thought little about it until about a year ago, when she began to realize the materials were integral to commemorating his legacy.
“I realized how much of the physical studio still existed through the paint tubes and brushes, and I felt a responsibility to preserve them as part of a record of his historical practice,” Barnes told Hyperallergic. “These tubes are the physical remnants of his creative process.”
Black figurative painters such as Jacob Lawrence, Amy Sherald, and Kerry James Marshall have been widely celebrated by museums and institutions in the last decade. Barnes isn’t always mentioned in the same breath as other contemporary art stars despite the $15.3 million sale of “The Sugar Shack” in 2022. (Its buyer, energy trader Bill Perkins, told the New York Times that “for certain segments of America, it’s more famous than the ‘Mona Lisa.’”)
That could soon change. A major documentary about Barnes’s life, Who is Ernie Barnes, was announced in July, and the Canton Museum of Art in Ohio recently opened a special exhibition celebrating his work, Good Times: The Artistic Journey of Ernie Barnes, on August 18. Some of Barnes’s works will also be on display at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which opens to the public on September 22.
Barnes grew up in Durham, North Carolina, under Jim Crow segregation, learning about art from books and catalogs because museums did not allow Black people to enter them. Encouraged by his mother, he sketched throughout his childhood and attended North Carolina College (now North Carolina Central University) on a football scholarship.
Barnes proved to be a gifted athlete in college and was drafted into the NFL, where he played for five seasons. But he never put aside his art and often made pencil or charcoal sketches of other players while he was on the sidelines during a game.
“His teammates were in awe of how he could come up with an idea and sketch it right away,” Thaleen Barnes, Ernie’s second wife, told Hyperallergic. “When we went to places, he watched how people walked, their mannerisms, and how they talked. He was interested in their body, their form and movement. Just looking around the world that we lived in was an inspiration for him to sketch.”

title: For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died: Priya Hajela on the trauma, contradictions of colonial history
content:
In the late 1970s and early 80s, in a school hall at The Lawrence School, Sanawar, students would rise together and recite Rudyard Kipling’s “The Children’s Song” — a pledge of loyalty to a motherland, sung in memory of fathers who had died defending it. Scattered through the rows were children who had recently lost fathers of their own, in wars with Pakistan. When the verse about fallen fathers landed, they would cry, and they would leave the hall. Priya Hajela, then a student at the school, never forgot it. “It made a huge impact on me,” she says.
Decades later, that hymn gave her the title of her new novel. For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died, published by Speaking Tiger, follows four generations of the Uppal family across nearly a century of upheaval, beginning after the death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and ending before the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
Speaking to The Indian Express, Hajela says her working title was Battle Lines, but once she finished the manuscript, she realised the book’s emotional charge was the relationship between fathers and sons. “The title has to touch the heart,” she says.
Hajela came to fiction rather late in life after a corporate career spanning 22 years. At 48, she pursued an MFA in creative writing at Goddard College in Vermont, which she completed in 2017, leading her to excavate the histories of her family and her people.
Born in Punjab, she was sent to boarding school at a young age and then moved to the United States at 17. Growing up, she could read Gurmukhi, but could not speak Punjabi fluently.
Her intention, she says, was never to study history for its own sake. “What drives me is actually to get an understanding of who I am and where I come from.”
Story continues below this ad
For Whose Dear Sake Our Fathers Died is a prequel to her earlier novel Ladies’ Tailor, which dealt with the aftermath of 1947. This time, the story is told through Beant Kaur as she pieces together the half-remembered life of her grandfather, Balwant Singh Uppal. “History talks about the leaders,” she said. “It doesn’t talk about what happened to the common man.”
A father’s death, a son’s dilemma
Balwant is where the novel’s central contradiction lives. He despises the East India Company as an “evil force,” but is willing to die for a British officer he personally serves.
The Calcutta army killed Balwant’s own father, a force made up overwhelmingly of Indian troops fighting under British command, says Hajela. “He wonders, are they my enemy, or are the British my enemy?” she says. “Yes, the British were leading, but there were so few of them.”
With the Sikh army his father died fighting for now dismantled, and farming crushed under rising taxes, joining the British Indian Army was the only option for Balwant.
Story continues below this ad
Hajela recounts the anguish of the Ferozepur Regiment, where Sikh soldiers were ordered to fight rebels who looked and spoke like them. They were so similar that they tore their turbans off, only to be torn apart on the battlefield. She says soldiers would turn their faces away as rebels were tied to cannons and blown apart. “There was definitely this massive guilt,” she said. “Is it really necessary? Yes, they rebelled. But to go to this length?”
Reading against the record
Getting the texture of this period right meant refusing to trust any single account, Hajela said. History written by the winners reads differently from history written by the losers, and until Independence, she points out, Indians lost at nearly every turn: the 1857 uprising, both Anglo-Sikh wars.
She found Indian-authored histories often eager to recover heroes and martyrs, while British accounts carried the victors’ biases, and she read the two against each other. Amarpal Singh’s histories of the first and second Anglo-Sikh wars became a key source; Singh, a computer engineer by training who became absorbed in this history, has also traced Sikh war memorials standing today in French fields from the First World War.
For the on-the-ground reality of 1857—what it actually felt like inside the Lucknow residency during the siege—Hajela turned to diaries written by British women, texts she found freely available.
Story continues below this ad
When the narrator doesn’t know everything
With all that research, Hajela’s first draft read like “a history textbook.” Her fix was to strip the story down to Balwant’s own limited vantage point.
“He does not know the rationale, and he does not know what’s happening elsewhere,” she says. “He is observing what is happening before him. And that is what he’s going to tell his granddaughter.”
She draws a direct line to her next project, a work of non-fiction on the Sikh Gurus. Guru Gobind Singh died in 1707, she said, but the Suraj Prakash, the chronicle by Kavi Santokh Singh that documents his life, was not written until the early 1800s.
For a century in between, the stories survived only by being retold and performed, gaining and shedding details with each telling. Hajela insists that the absence of a contemporaneous written record doesn’t make those stories less true.
Story continues below this ad
What’s left to fight for
Asked what she hopes readers take from the book, Hajela hopes it is the idea to “open your eyes, be aware, and find something to stand behind.”
She says the recent Gen Z student protests in Delhi against paper leaks were an example of the kind of stories worth telling.
“The world is becoming really strange,” she said. “You can’t just coast. Believe in something and believe strongly, and then do something for that cause.”
It’s advice Balwant himself gives his grandson in the novel: there may be no grand battles left to fight, but that doesn’t mean inaction is an option.
Story continues below this ad
Whether that instinct to act and pass the story on will survive in a generation fixated on their phones rather than a grandfather’s chair, Hajela isn’t sure. But she hopes the book does what that hymn in the Sanawar Hall once did to her: land somewhere and start a conversation.

title: El legado de las artistas trans que pusieron la ciudad de Las Palmas en la vanguardia
content: El Archivo ‘Viejas Glorias’ recupera la memoria escénica del colectivo trans en Gran Canaria entre 1976 y 1998 y rescata su aportación artística a un panorama cultural que despertaba de cuarenta años de dictaduraNueva ola de desabastecimiento de medicamentos para personas trans: “No podemos ser conejillos de indias” Cuando Luis Lorite se embarcó en la creación del Archivo Viejas Glorias, lo hizo bajo el convencimiento de que el legado artístico de las artistas trans y travestis desde 1976 no solo debe ser rescatado, sino celebrado. Todo parte de la búsqueda de testimonios y testigos de lo que fue un día una ciudad abierta al mundo por su puerto, que salía de una dictadura cruel de 40 años y de un colectivo de mujeres que quería probar todas las formas de libertad a través de la canción, la danza y el humor con la generosidad de situar a la ciudad de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria en un circuito cultural de repertorios y propuestas que se estaban dando en las salas y teatros del panorama internacional. Cartel 'Hollywood travesti' en la sala Britania. Las Palmas de Gran Canaria. “Este proyecto surge de una vieja gloria, Margaret García”, cuenta a esta redacción el coordinador del archivo. “La conocí haciendo una campaña del Orgullo para el Gobierno de Canarias en el año 2024, donde ella representaba al colectivo trans. Me comentó que había sido artista en una sala de fiestas de Las Palmas hacía cincuenta años y que tenía el sueño de volverse a encontrar con su público, que ella creía que, de tener su misma edad, estaría entonces en centros de mayores”. La artista trans Margaret Archivo 'Viejas Glorias'. El destino quiso que Margaret falleciera en la misma semana que el Instituto de las Mujeres del Ministerio de Igualdad les concedió la financiación para el proyecto, convirtiéndolo, del todo, en un homenaje a su memoria. “Ya no nos hacía falta más confirmación”. La dimensión artística Para Lorite, que ha trabajado toda su vida en las artes escénicas, era crucial que este proyecto restituyera a las artistas trans una dimensión a veces secuestrada por la visión que de ellas se tiene como víctimas o supervivientes. Expandir la mirada y ver la aportación que legaron y la calidad de sus espectáculos para atrapar a un público estando más de diez años en cartel. Carla Antonelli. “Tenía la hipótesis, y la he confirmado, de que eran artistas, creadoras, intérpretes, que luego tuvieron mucho éxito. En la sala Britania, llenaron de domingo a martes durante más de una década, haciendo hasta dos pases y trayendo guaguas de turistas desde el Sur”. La valentía de ser ellas Decía el poeta griego Píndaro que ojalá todos los humanos lleguen a ser quienes realmente son. A veces se tarda toda una vida y otras veces no se llega a tiempo. Las viejas glorias tuvieron la valentía de apostarlo todo a la libertad y a ser quienes realmente fueron a un precio a veces muy alto, para ir cien pasos por delante de quienes en público las criticaban y en privado las envidiaban. “Representaban ese cambio de piel del país entero como nadie, con una mirada curiosa, que va más allá de lo artístico. Representaban qué se podía hacer con esa nueva libertad que estaba estrenando el país. La libertad en potencia después de cuarenta años de castración moral, mental y cultural. Esas mujeres cogieron esa libertad y la dinamitaron”. Un archivo en construcción, memoria de convivencia Aunque el trabajo de recopilación de Viejas Glorias, presentado esta semana en Gran Canaria, se ha centrado en el periodo comprendido entre 1976 y 1998, no pretende ser un relato cerrado sino seguir recopilando archivos, fotografías, programas, cartelería y continuando ese diálogo entre público y artistas. “Todas las fotografías que están en el proyecto y que se pueden ver en la página web reflejan a personas que están viviendo en su ciudad, moviéndose entre la gente. Por ejemplo, Sandy, que además de intérprete era costurera, que cosía para el carnaval, y en esa se eliminan los prejuicios”. Sandy, artista trans del barrio de Las Rehoyas y costurera. Luis Lorite invita a todas aquellas personas que quieran contribuir con material a hacerlo a través del formulario web del archivo. Esta redacción termina la entrevista preguntándole si el arte debe ser transformador: “Es la única razón para hacer arte”, sentencia.

title: 2 Negrense national artists: One painted people’s struggles, the other lit the stage
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Nunelucio Alvarado and Teodoro Hilado were named among the National Artists for 2025, recognizing their significant contributions to art and theater in the Philippines.
- Alvarado, a social-realist artist, has dedicated over five decades to portraying the lives of ordinary people, while Hilado, known as the 'Father of Philippine Lighting Design,' pioneered technical direction in theater.
- Both artists have left a lasting impact on their communities, with Alvarado continuing to live among those he inspires, and Hilado being honored posthumously for his innovative work in enhancing theatrical storytelling.
NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – One is 76 and living with dementia in his hometown, where for more than five decades he turned his art toward the lives and struggles of people around him. The other died in 2015, after a career devoted to an aspect of theater most audiences rarely see but experience in every production.
Nunelucio Alvarado, fondly called “Maestro Nunelucio,” and Teodoro “Teddy” Ledesma-Hilado were named among the 10 National Artists for 2025 in Proclamation No. 1414 announced by Malacañang on Wednesday, September 9.
Their recognition brings together two very different lives in art. Alvarado is the social-realist artist from Sagay whose provocative works became a quiet form of social revolution, while Hilado, the Silaynon known as the “Father of Philippine Lighting Design,” pioneered lighting design and technical direction in the Philippines.
For Helen Arguelles Cutillar, Sagay’s tourism and information officer, Alvarado’s life is itself a canvas.
“He is peerless,” Cutillar said. “He touched people’s lives, especially the poor in so many ways.”
Alvarado has no college degree. Yet for more than five decades, he etched his mark in visual arts, building a body of work centered on social realities and the lives of ordinary people.
His recognition, however, is not being seen in Sagay as a distinction that belongs to him alone.
Sagay Mayor Leo Rafael Cueva said the honor also belongs to the communities whose lives and struggles have been at the heart of Alvarado’s work.
“Maestro Nunelucio showed that an artist does not have to leave his community behind to create work that matters to the nation and the world,” Cueva said. “He brought his art back to Sagay, shared it with our children and communities, and helped make art part of everyday life here.”
“We now have a national treasure living with us. He is a true gem in the field of arts,” Negros Occidental 2nd District Representative Alfredo Marañon III said on Thursday, September 10.
Alvarado is living with dementia, and his wife, Rosalia “Sally” Alvarado, spoke on behalf of the family as the country recognized his contribution.
“We hope his legacy of bringing art and the love for art into the community will continue for generations to come,” she said.
The Metropolitan Museum of Manila hailed the declaration of Alvarado as a national artist, saying it highlighted his work depicting the lives and struggles of communities in Negros.
It said Alvarado has been known for his social realist works rooted in the sugarlands of Negros, with recurring images of sakadas and sugarcane reflecting exploitation, hardship, resistance, survival and hope.
The museum, which holds Alvarado’s works in its collection, said his art has given voice to local communities and helped bring their experiences and stories to a wider audience.
“Immortalizing his agrarian activism in his work, Alvarado continues to spread his philosophy that art belongs to the people and his advocacy for the active involvement of art and grassroots communities in the Philippines,” read part of the museum’s statement.
The museum also celebrated the declaration of another national artist, Imelda Cajipe-Endaya (visual arts), whose works are also in its collection.
The museum said Endaya is known for her textured mixed-media works using everyday fabrics and objects, and for an artistic practice focused on Filipino identity, human rights, feminism, overseas Filipino workers, environmental issues and peace.
“Their works have illuminated the realities, struggles, and aspirations of local communities and through their art and advocacy, Cajipe-Endaya and Alvarado have made impactful contributions to Philippine art and inspire future generations to learn and appreciate the stories that shape them as Filipinos,” it said.
If Alvarado brought art into the life of his community, Hilado devoted his career to the technical side of theater.
The Silay-born artist was named a national artist for theater, specifically for technical direction, 11 years after his death at 77, recognizing a career that helped establish technical direction as an important part of theater from the wings.
Hilado pioneered lighting design and technical direction in the Philippines and became known as the “Father of Philippine Lighting Design.”
He helped professionalize the technical side of the performing arts, using light, space and technical direction to enhance storytelling.
When he served as technical director at the Cultural Center of the Philippines, Hilado mastered a minimalist approach to theater, using lights and space to heighten storytelling. His work created atmospheres that captivated audiences and helped raise the standards of local productions to an international level.
Silay Mayor Joedith Gallego asked Silaynons to celebrate Hilado’s recognition.
“He [was] an exceptional artist behind theater lighting and productions,” Gallego said.
Hilado was the third national artist from Silay, according to Solomon Locsin, chairman of the Negros Occidental Historical Council. Before him came Leandro Locsin, who was declared a national artist for architecture in 1990, and Agnes Dakudao-Locsin, national artist for dance in 2022.
In Sagay, the recognition of Alvarado brings national attention to an artist whose work has remained closely tied to his community. And in Silay, Hilado’s posthumous recognition honors a career devoted to the technical craft of theater.
Their lives in art were different. One continues to live with the community that became central to his work; the other is remembered for a career that helped shape how theater was presented to audiences.
Aside from Alvarado, Hilado and Endaya, the other 2025 national artists are as follows:
- Gabriel “Gabby” Formoso – architecture
- Rafael “Nonoy” Catalino Froilan – dance
- Maria Beatriz “Patis” Fabella Pamintuan Tesoro – design and allied arts
- Armando “Bing” Lao – film and broadcast arts
- Gregorio Brillantes – literature
- Nicanor Tiongson – literature
- Alfredo Buenaventura – music

title: Amid war, Ukrainian soldiers celebrate love at ritual wedding
content:
Amid war, Ukrainian soldiers celebrate love at ritual wedding
KYIV – As twilight settled on a hillside by the river near the eastern Ukrainian front, two soldiers exchanged wedding vows during a Slavic ritual honouring ancestors and fallen warriors.
Torches lit the way for the 30-year-old groom, known by the call-sign Ice, and the 32-year-old bride, Khomochka, through the woods to the altar as fellow soldiers formed a guard of honour.
“Before our brothers-in-arms and ancestors, before those no longer with us and those who stand before us, we speak this oath,” they said in unison as the ceremony began.
Combining pagan Slavic traditions and Orthodox Christianity, the Mysteriya ritual revived by the Azov brigade serves as the formal ceremonial framework for the unit’s most significant moments.
Branches were draped with colourful ribbons and ritual wreaths, while bonfires blazed high, ready for the military brotherhood to gather around them.
The ceremony also drew uninvited guests.
Right before the event started, several long-distance drones, usually sent to strike enemy territory, buzzed over the gathering.
Celebrations still went ahead.
More than 4½ years into Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, moments of peace and joy have become especially valuable to the soldiers.
“Events like this show that not everything ends with war – that life goes on,” said Dmytro Rogoziuk, the commander of the 60th Brigade.
“To be honest, for me personally as a commander, there are very few events that bring genuine joy.”
‘I swear’
Though they had been legally married for a year, the couple saw the paperwork as a mere formality, compared with the solemn vows they exchanged before fellow soldiers with whom they had fought for a decade and shared life-and-death risks.
Their daily reality was now manpower shortage, Russian offensives, lack of leave, dangerous rotations to the front lines and reports of their friends’ deaths.
While the exact death toll of this war is unknown, various estimates suggest the casualties number in the tens or even hundreds of thousands.
Khomochka managed the unit’s medical service, carrying the heavy load of trying to save the wounded.
“She’s unstoppable, like a live wire,” said Ice, whose blue eyes – which gave him his call-sign – warmed up when he looked at his wife.
He ended his vows saying: “Your honour shall become my honour; your home shall become my home.”
Khomochka repeated, word for word.
With one voice, they declared to the assembly.
“Such is our word, such is our oath. I swear!”
Their friends and brothers-in-arms loudly proclaimed they accepted the oath.
“If we don’t live here and now, then when should we live, when we are in a state of war?” Khomochka said. AFP

title: [Magazine] En Corée du Sud, la relève chez les «femmes de la mer»
content:
Les haenyeo, ou «femmes de la mer», sont un symbole de liberté, de respect de la nature et de résilience féminine dans une Corée du Sud profondément patriarcale. Si cette tradition ne peut freiner son déclin, une nouvelle génération de plongeuses se forme.
Jin So-hee a gagné sa place parmi les plongeuses sud-coréennes qui récoltent des fruits de mer au prix de durs efforts. Elle fait partie à présent d’une nouvelle génération qui perpétue une tradition vieille de plusieurs siècles. La transformation économique rapide de la Corée du Sud a fait fondre le nombre de «femmes de la mer», ou «haenyeo», qui plongent en apnée pour récolter des fruits de mer. Cette profession proche de la nature mais très physique attire à nouveau des recrues, échaudées par un monde du travail sud-coréen déshumanisant.
Jin So-hee, 33 ans, a grandi à Busan, deuxième plus grande ville du pays, et a obtenu des diplômes d’esthéticienne et manucure avant de travailler comme aide-infirmière pour gagner sa vie. Découragée par la compétition au travail, des journées à rallonge et un maigre salaire, elle a décidé de mettre le cap vers la ville côtière de Geoje à l’âge de 25 ans. Elle y a rencontré des haenyeo septuagénaires et a été attirée par leur liberté et leur travail en communion avec la nature jusqu’à un âge avancé.
Au début, la jeune femme dit avoir perdu sept kilos en plongeant et avoir parfois été si fatiguée qu’elle «avait à peine la force de tenir une cuillère». Les haenyeo plongent avec pour seule protection une combinaison et des lunettes, qu’elles enduisent de salive et d’armoise pour éviter la buée, comme le veut la tradition. Elle a souffert de douleurs aux oreilles dues à la pression de l’eau, et de sévères migraines, des maux rencontrés par des générations de haenyeo. «La douleur était si forte que j’en avais les larmes aux yeux (…) je ne pouvais rien entendre.» Déterminée, Jin So-hee a appris des techniques modernes de plongée en apnée et en bouteille visant à égaliser la pression dans ses oreilles.
Pourquoi est-ce que je me battais si férocement en ville?
Choi Young-hee, 60 ans
Les haenyeo, dont le savoir-faire est classé au patrimoine culturel immatériel de l’humanité par l’Unesco, sont devenues un symbole d’indépendance et de résilience féminines dans un pays profondément patriarcal. Sur l’île de Jeju, au cœur de cette tradition, le nombre de haenyeo est tombé à 2 371 l’année dernière, contre 3 437 en 2021. Mais cette tradition existe ailleurs, notamment à Geoje.
S’intégrer à cette communauté des haenyeo plus âgées de Geoje a été un nouveau défi pour Jin So-hee et Woo Jung-min, autre plongeuse de la nouvelle génération. Les plongeuses se méfiaient de ces jeunes qui filmaient leur vie et publiaient des vidéos sur YouTube. «Nous voulions documenter le fait qu’il existe des jeunes haenyeo comme nous, pour que cela puisse un jour devenir une sorte d’archive et peut-être même un atout pour les générations futures», explique Woo Jung-mi, 40 ans.
Choi Young-hee, 60 ans, est devenue haenyeo à la fin de la quarantaine après avoir été pendant deux décennies vendeuse dans des grands magasins de Séoul. En visitant Geoje, elle a aperçu des silhouettes dans la mer qui plongeaient et remontaient sans cesse. Croyant d’abord qu’il s’agissait de dauphins, elle a compris ensuite que c’était des haenyeo. Fascinée, cette expérience l’a amenée à remettre sa vie en question, se demandant : «Pourquoi est-ce que je me battais si férocement en ville?» Aujourd’hui, elle dirige une association qui enseigne la culture des haenyeo et forme les futures plongeuses.
Malgré quelques jeunes recrues, le nombre de haenyeo ne cesse de diminuer. Le réchauffement de la mer perturbe les écosystèmes marins, raréfie les prises et rend leur dangereuse profession encore plus précaire. Un seul trou minuscule dans une combinaison de plongée peut être critique dans la mer glaciale en hiver, explique Woo Jung-mi. «Tu gagnes ta vie dans le royaume des morts et tu la passes dans le monde des vivants», dit un ancien dicton des haenyeo. «La mer est tellement dangereuse, et l’épuisement physique et mental si fort, que nous le considérons pratiquement comme l’au-delà», confie la quadragénaire.
Mais pour les deux plongeuses, la beauté saisissante de la mer vaut tous les efforts. Même si cette beauté elle-même s’estompe avec le changement climatique. Ainsi, les ascidies rouges – des invertébrés marins en forme de sac – qui transformaient le fond de l’océan en «champ de roses» chaque printemps, ont disparu, déplore Jin So-hee.

title: Disability advocate's tragic drowning spurs life-saving gesture
content:
Family and friends have paid tribute to disability advocate Ellen Fraser-Barbour, who died in April at a Northern Territory swimming hole.
First responders unveiled an automated external defibrillator and plaque at Ellery Creek Big Hole, 80 kilometres west of Alice Springs, in Dr Fraser-Barbour's honour.
Her mother, Susie Fraser, thanked St John Ambulance service for its initiative to provide a potentially life-saving device in a remote location.
A small but intimate ceremony was held at Ellery Creek Big Hole only five months after the death of disability advocate Ellen Fraser-Barbour, who tragically drowned while swimming in April this year.
Her mother, Susie Fraser, family and friends travelled to the site to unveil an automated external defibrillator (AED) and a plaque to honour the work and memory of Dr Fraser-Barbour.
Ms Fraser took the opportunity to thank the first responders and St John Ambulance service for providing the defibrillator.
"I'd like to thank you all for your initiative in doing this and for finding some way of making something positive come out of something which was so tragic,"
she said.
"I think your will and determination to do this is incredibly important to us and that something positive can come out of something so shocking."
Closure for family
William Sears, duty manager at Alice Springs Ambulance Station, was involved in Dr Fraser-Barbour's care.
"It was a tough day for ambulance because of the challenges involved in providing emergency healthcare in remote Central Australia," he said.
"There is no aeromedical response, so the next closest ambulance response is roughly an hour via road."
Mr Sears said Dr Fraser-Barbour's family was supportive of the gesture to commemorate the work she had done in the disability sector.
"It's a good opportunity to not only provide some life-saving equipment in remote Central Australia, but to offer the family some closure and some help with their journey."
Abbey Studley, regional manager for St John Ambulance Northern Territory, said it was an honour to be included at the commemoration.
"It's not often, if not ever, that frontline workers get to speak with families after tragedies or even be a part of any commemoration services, and so it also forms part of our grieving process," she said.
"I think Dr Ellen Fraser Barber was a big believer in equal rights and something as simple as providing an AED in an area that doesn't normally have it, I think aligns really well with who she was."
Deeply missed
At the time of her death, the 35-year-old was championed as a passionate disability advocate who loved travelling and hiking.
Dr Fraser-Barbour's sister Harriet shared the impact on her family and the community in a statement to the ABC.
"Ellen was a fierce and defiant force who made a lasting impact on all that she encountered," she said.
"We cannot describe the hole she will leave in our family, and she will be missed greatly by her community.
"She was an amazing friend to many and wise beyond her years with so much left to give.
"Ellen helped to shape so much of who I am today, and I will not be the same without her."

title: With joy and grief, Palestinian football marks return
content:
AL-RAM (PALESTINIAN TERRITORIES) - Palestinian sports commentator Khalil Jadallah has spent the past three years mourning the athletes killed in the Gaza war. As Palestinian football officially resumed this week, his return to the stadium proved bittersweet.
Palestinian professional sports were brought to a halt after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, in which 1,014 Palestinian athletes were killed, according to the Palestinian Football Association's tally.
On Friday, Jadallah was back at Faisal Al-Husseini Stadium in Al-Ram in the West Bank to call the opening match of the first tournament organised by the association in three years.
Though long awaited, the event was marked by contradicting emotions for Jadallah: "a feeling of joy at returning after such an absence, but also a feeling of loss.
"We lost players... fans, administrators and referees," Jadallah told AFP.
- '1,000 Martyrs Cup' -
The football association named the comeback tournament -- which includes over 200 teams from the occupied West Bank, Gaza, and refugee camps in Lebanon -- the "1,000 Martyrs Cup".
Throughout the war, Palestinian football authorities have accused Israel of killing football players and damaging Gaza's sporting infrastructure.
Israel has said 12 Palestinian football figures that it killed in Gaza, including a FIFA-registered referee, were members of militant groups, an allegation the football association has rejected.
Large numbers of Palestinian security forces were deployed for the event, an unusual sight in the town more accustomed to Israeli military raids.
Before the game, pitting Jabal Al-Mukaber Club against Shabab Al-Khaleel SC, children carried a Palestinian flag wrapped to resemble a dead body, before unfurling it across the centre circle as a band played the Palestinian national anthem.
The sport authority also unveiled a memorial bearing the names of the killed Palestinian athletes outside the stadium, which stands in Al-Ram, not far from the West Bank separation barrier.
Samir Issa a prominent former player and veteran manager who had coached both teams, watched from the stands as the game kicked off.
"Football has become more important than politics today," he said. "The proof of that is the following the World Cup has had."
"Sport in general is the culture of the people," he added, saying that Palestinians had "the right to practice sport normally and in all its forms, not just football".
At the 10-minute, 14-second mark, the referee ordered the game to stop for a minute of silence for the dead before the crowd grew loud again.
"Football returns to Palestine," read electronic screens around the stadium.
Thousands of mainly young people attended the game, with families, women and children seated in a separate section.
Maysan Suleiman, a 35-year-old from Al-Ram, said she came to commemorate "the martyrs".
- 'Football returns to Palestine' -
"I don't support either team," she said. "I came to support the idea (of the tournament) itself. After all, they're all sons of Palestine."
The tournament opened simultaneously in Gaza, where Israeli strikes have left much of the territory in ruins and some football fields have been turned into makeshift camps for those displaced by the war.
The opening match there was held in Deir al-Balah between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah as fans sat on plastic chairs around the small field lined with palm trees.
"Football represented life for us before the war, and after the war the lives of players stopped altogether," said Khalil Matar, a Khadamat Rafah player.
Matar said holding the cup simultaneously in the West Bank, Gaza and refugee camps in Lebanon reflected "national unity" for Palestinians.
But the West Bank teams are set to face major logistical hurdles as they travel between cities and Israeli military checkpoints in the occupied territory.
"Still, we're determined to continue sporting activities and developing our young people," said Abdullah Abu Ghassan of the Shabab Jaba team competing in the tournament.

title: Público puede acceder gratis a cómic bilingüe con 4 relatos del pueblo Nomatsigenga
content:
Cuatro relatos tradicionales del pueblo indígena u originario Nomatsigenga cobran vida en un cómic bilingüe que el Ministerio de Cultura pone a disposición del público de manera gratuita a través del Centro de Recursos Interculturales. Se trata de Igengitsare Nomatsigenga: Relatos Nomatsigenga, una publicación elaborada de manera participativa junto con integrantes de este pueblo de la región Junín.


El cómic reúne cuatro historias: “Imoro santani otisikë mogobati - La cueva del guácharo en el cerro Mogobati”, “Tsinane janainaro pobigëri sekari - La mujer enferma que envenenó al tigre”, “Opoata patyarija - La poza de sal” e “Ira pagitsa - El águila”.
Los relatos están basados en narraciones orales recopiladas en la comunidad nativa San Antonio de Sonomoro, ubicada en el distrito de Pangoa, provincia de Satipo. Fueron seleccionados por su contenido cultural, social y simbólico y posteriormente adaptados al formato de cómic, ilustrados y traducidos al nomatsigenga.
La publicación busca contribuir a la transmisión de estas historias a las nuevas generaciones, así como fortalecer el uso, valoración y preservación de la lengua y cultura Nomatsigenga. Asimismo, se desarrolla en el contexto de la Política Nacional de Lenguas Originarias, Tradición Oral e Interculturalidad al 2040 y la Política Nacional de la Lectura, el Libro y las Bibliotecas al 2030.
El proceso de elaboración tomó aproximadamente seis meses y se desarrolló de manera participativa entre el pueblo Nomatsigenga y el Ministerio de Cultura. En una primera etapa se recopilaron diversas narraciones orales compartidas por narradores locales. A partir de este material se seleccionaron cuatro relatos, que fueron adaptados al formato de cómic considerando aspectos narrativos, visuales y lingüísticos.
Posteriormente, las versiones en nomatsigenga y las ilustraciones fueron validadas con integrantes del propio pueblo a través de talleres realizados en la Comunidad Nativa San Antonio de Sonomoro, como parte del proceso de elaboración de la publicación.
El cómic puede consultarse de manera gratuita en el Centro de Recursos Interculturales del Ministerio de Cultura:
https://shorturl.at/ot2Af
Historias que se mantienen vivas
Las tradiciones orales pueden presentar distintas versiones de una misma historia, debido a que cada comunidad o familia puede conservar su propia manera de contarla. Por ello, el cómic no busca establecer una versión única u oficial de los relatos, sino recoger las versiones compartidas durante el proceso participativo.
De esta manera, la publicación acerca estas narraciones a públicos de distintas edades mediante un formato visual y bilingüe, y contribuye a poner en valor la memoria colectiva, los conocimientos y las expresiones culturales del pueblo Nomatsigenga.

title: Boy's football ground challenge for 'heart of gold' mum
content:
Boy's football ground challenge for 'heart of gold' mum
- Published
A 10-year-old Dundee boy is completing ten laps of every professional football pitch in Scotland in memory of his late mother.
Jacob McDonald is walking around the 42 grounds to raise money and awareness in honour of his mum Vivienne, who died of a rare lung disease aged 32, when Jacob was 18-months-old.
Jacob's Ground Journeys will see him and his father Kenny travel more than 6,000 miles (9,656km) from Ross County to Stranraer with all the stops in between.
The duo have completed 18 football grounds so far, including Celtic, Rangers, and St Mirren.
Kenny said Jacob was excited at the prospect of the challenge.
He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "He likes to be adventurous, looking at different places, and being a typical 10-year-old boy as well, he loves the attention.
"It's just been phenomenal."
Jacob became an ambassador for the Pulmonary Fibrosis Trust when he was seven.
The condition is incurable and is progressive, and the general prognosis is between three and five years.
His ground journey challenge has raised about £6,500 so far.
Jacob said: "It's been so much fun so far.
"Some of the pitches are massive and my legs get really tired, but I just think about my mum and keep going.
"My favourite ground so far was East Kilbride because everyone was so supportive. Dad jokes I walk faster than him now."
Jacob has met players including Dundee's Simon Murray and former Celtic player Charlie Mulgrew and the Edinburgh City players applauded him on his final lap, which Kenny said was "a lovely touch."
Kenny said clubs and businesses across the country had been "incredibly generous".
Jacob has sensory issues, finding bright light and noise difficult to be around, and wears ear defenders, with Kenny accompanying him at all times.
Kenny said Vivienne, who was diagnosed with the disease when she was 28, had a "heart of gold".
He said Vivienne became pregnant despite being told she could never have children.
"It was quite difficult, knowing Vivienne was going to pass and I was going to be left with Jacob," he said.
"And to be fair, the whole time that Vivienne was carrying Jacob we never spoke about her mortality.
"We just got on with it, she was happy, I was happy."
Kenny said that after Vivienne's funeral he had been sorting her belongings.
He said: "Unbeknownst to me, she'd left all these letters for myself and Jacob around the house that she knew we would find, for us to read.
"She's written letters for Jacob's milestones for his 16th, 18th, his 21st birthday.
"Other letters he's got, I'm going to wait until he starts high school, then I'm going to let him open them and have a proper read, so he understands more."

title: In turbulent times, football brings Haiti hope
content:
In Haiti, the sport of football creates social cohesion: despite their differences, people from all classes come together on the field. Children from wealthy families, poor backgrounds, and middle-class homes alike get the opportunity to mix by either playing for the same football team, or facing one another as opponents.
The same approach informs how players are chosen for the national team; all social categories are represented based solely on the quality of each player’s talent. Spectators have a similar experience, in that people from all walks of life cross paths to celebrate, support their teams, and share moments of victory or defeat.
Naturally, the security crisis that has displaced more than a million people internally and caused thousands of deaths over the last six years has affected every sector of national life. This includes sport in general and football, in particular, since “the beautiful game” is a passion for almost all ages and social groups in Haiti.
Despite the country’s lack of modern sports infrastructure, you can see people of every generation playing football everywhere: on school grounds, in the streets, on unpaved fields, in yards and corridors, and in sports parks across the country. For young people from poor and disadvantaged neighbourhoods, football offers an opportunity to join local semi-professional clubs and maybe even play at national level.
Since the gang violence has escalated, however, much of the country’s main infrastructure has been damaged through looting, fire, or other means, and sports facilities have not been spared. The FIFA Goal Center in Croix-des-Bouquets, for instance, which trained stars like Melchie Dumornay (Corventina) of Olympique Lyonnais in France, Nérilia Mondésir of Seattle Reign FC in the United States, and Kethna Louis of Montpellier HSC in France, was attacked, looted, and burned by the 400 Mawozo gang led by Wilson Joseph (alias Lanmò San Jou).
Likewise, the Sylvio Cator Stadium in southern Port-au-Prince, the home of Haitian national football, and the Haitian Olympic Center in Croix-des-Missions in the city's north, where many young people would train in different sports, suffered major gang attacks in February 2024 and February 2026, respectively. The area around the Sylvio Cator Stadium is controlled by two powerful gangs, one led by Renel Destina (alias “Ti Lapli” or “Kaporal Lapli”) and the other by Johnson André (alias “Izo 5 Second”). The Olympic Center area is controlled by Claudy Célestin (alias “Chen Mechan” or “Stevenson Pierre”) of the Chen Mechan (“Mean Dog,” in English) gang in Plaine-du-Cul-de-Sac, and Jeff Larose (alias Jeff Gwo Lwa) of the Taliban gang based in Canaan.
Because criminal gangs control the main roads leading to the country's Great South and Great North, the regular national championship has halted, forcing the national football league to adapt and organise a special competition so players can keep playing. Many sports parks are located in areas controlled by gangs, which makes the situation worse.
Despite all this, Haitian football is not dead. On November 18, 2025, the Grenadiers qualified for the 2026 World Cup, even though no qualifying match was played in Haiti because of the gang violence. Although the national team was eliminated in the first round of the World Cup, their participation brought joy to the Haitian people.
The sport continues to put smiles on people’s faces in Haiti. In this year’s Caribbean Football Union (CFU) U14 Challenge Series, which ended on August 23 in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, the Haitian U14 team won the tournament with a series of brilliant performances.
They beat Trinidad and Tobago 4-1 and French Guiana 5-2, lost 1-0 to Puerto Rico (after already qualifying for the semifinals), defeated the host nation 6-1 in the semifinals, and beat Jamaica 4-0 in the final to become Division 1 champions. This victory marked Haiti’s third CFU U14 title, following their previous championship wins in 2021 and 2022. All three titles were secured during a time when the country was going through a crisis.
To help these young players participate in the tournament, the Haitian Football Federation (FHF) organised a talent detection tournament across various regions of the island, with participation from several football academies. Young footballers were enrolled in a two-month preparation camp at the Dulaire Sports Complex/Training Center, in the municipality of Ouanaminthe and, more specifically, in the communal section of Haut-Maribahoux, a border area near Dajabón in the Dominican Republic.
The young champions returned home on Monday, August 24, to a welcome reception at the diplomatic lounge of the Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince, organised by the Ministry of Youth, Sports, and Civic Action (MJSAC).
During the ceremony, the Minister of Sports highlighted individual performances, including Jerry Petit-Homme, who scored a goal just four or five seconds into the match against the Dominican Republic — one of the fastest goals in football history. Wensley Dumorné was named the Best Player of Division 1, and Jodley Sheeckensley Delmas was named top scorer, with seven goals.
Team captain Cedric Clairemond shared a warm message with Haitian football fans, on behalf of all the players:
Moun yo mèsi anpil pou lamou nou, jodi a nou chanpyon nou ba nou koup la, mwen fyè anpil paske mwen reprezante peyi'm antan ke kapitèn, sa fè de mwa n ap prepare, nou te motive pou sa, tout objektif la se te chanpyon jodi a nou fè'l, nou swete pou nou rejwi de koup la, ti grenadye yo ap vini pou nou monte pi wo.
Thank you everyone so much for your love. Today we are champions and we bring you the trophy. I am very proud to represent my country as captain. We prepared for two months and were very motivated. The goal was to become champions, and today we did it. We hope you enjoy this trophy; the young Grenadiers are coming to reach even higher levels.
Sports Minister Phytagore Dumas stated his commitment to supporting these young players in their education and personal growth. According to a statement from his ministry, the young Grenadiers won on the field, and it is now up to the nation to support them towards a future worthy of their talent.
The Haitian Football Federation echoed this sentiment:
Aktivite jodi a se te pou temwanye yo lanmou ak sipò, pou renouvle angajman nou pou kontinye batay pou leve nivo foutbòl la nan peyi a epi garanti relèv la. Objektif la pa t lòt, se mize sou jenès la jodi a pou reyalize rèv demen yo.
Today’s event was to show them love and support, and to renew our commitment to keep fighting to raise the level of football in the country and secure the future. The objective was simple: invest in today’s youth to achieve tomorrow’s dreams.
Haiti’s U17 national team is currently preparing at Parc Sainte-Claire in Delmas for the 20th edition of the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Qatar, training and playing friendly matches against local teams to get ready for the tournament, which takes place from November 19 to December 13. Meanwhile, the U20s narrowly missed qualification for the FIFA U-20 World Cup in Chile. On August 31, however, the same team qualified for the men’s football tournament of the 2027 Pan American Games, to be held in Lima, Peru. Haiti earned its spot as the highest-ranked Caribbean team following its performance in the recent Concacaf U-20 Championship.
Yet, because of the ongoing violence, especially in the metropolitan area of Port-au-Prince, Haiti itself cannot celebrate as it would like. Even with the U14s’ great performance, the joy did not last long. On the night of August 24, fewer than 24 hours after their victory, armed gangs from the criminal group Viv Ansanm killed around 47 people and kidnapped more than 30 others, including young girls, women, and seniors in the municipality of Kenscoff, a mountain town near the capital.
In spite of the challenges, good things keep happening every day in the country. You can see it in culture, art, farming projects, entrepreneurship and sport, especially in parts of the country not under gang control. Perhaps that is football’s most enduring lesson — that in spite of obstacles, you must keep moving forward.

title: India's Kerala gets nearly 40 snake rescue calls a day, and 2,952 volunteers charge nothing
content:
Kerala, India, handles around 40 snake rescues a day, free of charge.
Here's what to know
Kerala faces an astonishing volume of human-wildlife encounters, with nearly 40 snake rescues every day, according to The New Indian Express.
Across Kerala, many of those calls are handled by volunteers who do the work for free, removing snakes from yards, vehicles, kitchens, storerooms, and other ordinary places while trying to protect both residents and the animals.
Kerala now uses its Snake Awareness, Rescue and Protection Application (SARPA), as a key part of its response to snake sightings to give people access to a trained rescuer who can capture it and release it back into its habitat.
Since the program began in August 2020, forest department figures show 105,696 sighting reports and 87,708 rescues. Some of the snakes handled through the program are protected under Schedule I and II of the Wildlife Protection Act.
Mission SARPA nodal officer Muhammad Anvar Yunus said, "Keralam's dense settlements and proximity to natural habitats mean encounters with snakes are common. A snake inside a house or compound can trigger fear, leading to attempts to kill it. Instead, (via SARPA) residents alert the rescue network, following which a certified volunteer reaches the spot, captures the snake and relocates it to a suitable habitat. The system has helped shift focus from eliminating snakes to managing encounters with them safely."
More background
The New Indian Express reported that SARPA's statewide network of 2,952 certified volunteers helps the system respond quickly when snake sightings trigger panic. They go to places they may not know, sometimes deal with venomous species, and pay their own travel costs, all while offering the service free to the public.
What's being done?
Forest department officials say the state is considering added support for rescuers, including a travel allowance to offset the cost of reaching rescue sites and an insurance scheme that reflects the risks of the work.
A volunteer from Palakkad told The New Indian Express, "We are taught to rescue a snake scientifically and without risk. However, there is still some risk involved while dealing with venomous snakes. We also request providing snake catching kits to all certified volunteers."
Where can I learn more?
Similar encounters are playing out elsewhere, from cobra removals inside Indian homes to growing concern over snakebites as temperatures climb. They also highlight the overlap between rescue work and conservation when dangerous animals need to be moved carefully and returned to the wild.
• In Telangana, India, an Indian cobra relocation turned a frightening home encounter into a safe release.
• Across India, rising temperatures and snakebites are raising fears of a worsening public health crisis.
• In the Philippines, rescuers freed an injured python and a water monitor after earlier captivity.
• In Louisiana, conservationists released rare pine snake hatchlings to rebuild a species under pressure.
Each case points to the same basic lesson: when people and snakes share space, trained rescue, safe relocation, and long-term conservation all matter.

title: North Carolina county gets $23 million as PFAS polluters pay for cleaner water
content:
Robeson County, North Carolina, is expected to receive nearly $23 million for clean-water work under a major PFAS settlement. The funding follows decades of contamination tied to chemical manufacturers throughout the state.
Here's what to know
North Carolina says it has reached a $590 million agreement with DuPont, Chemours, and Corteva. The deal, announced by North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson and North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality Secretary Reid Wilson, is intended to address the contamination of state waters by per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
According to local outlet WMBF News, Robeson County is projected to get close to $23 million over time, including roughly $2.3 million in the first year. The overall package includes a $455 million settlement payout and a $135 million reserve fund, making it the largest environmental-damages recovery in state history.
County officials told the station the money is planned for public-water treatment upgrades, including advanced filtration, and for continued landfill analysis and monitoring. They also said a pilot program is already underway at the Rocco Water Treatment Plant as broader infrastructure improvements continue.
Jackson described the settlement as a way to make the companies answer for harm done in North Carolina.
"It is a massive step forward in giving our state more dollars to help fund clean water programs," Jackson said in the announcement. "This settlement puts even more teeth behind the consent order with NCDEQ. Chemours made this mess, and we're making sure Chemours cleans it up."
PFAS are a class of human-made chemicals that can persist in habitats and human bodies for long periods.
More background
The North Carolina case centers on contamination associated with the Fayetteville Works facility. The settlement announcement noted DuPont began operating the site in the early 1970s and used southeastern North Carolina as a PFAS dumping ground.
More than 500,000 people in the area rely on the Cape Fear River for drinking water, according to WMBF News, and the watershed is also important for farming and recreation. State researchers found very high PFAS concentrations there in a late-2016 study.
State efforts to curb the pollution began almost 10 years ago. Then, in 2019, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality secured an order to mandate that Chemours stop wastewater discharges, reduce air pollution from GenX and other PFAS, provide filtration for people with contaminated drinking water wells, cut PFAS pollution in the Cape Fear River, and address contamination sources at the facility.
What's being done?
The settlement provides funding for a range of local governments and utilities. WMBF reported that the money will help pay for filtration and other cleanup work intended to make household water safer.
According to the local outlet, the agreement is separate from a federal lawsuit filed in June that alleges groundwater feeding the Rocco plant was contaminated by Robeson County's landfill, not Chemours' Fayetteville Works. Still, the county said it will keep moving ahead with efforts to improve water quality.
"This settlement provides our county with the critical, dedicated resources needed to ensure that our residents have the safest drinking and household use water possible," officials said, per WMBF.
Where can I learn more?
This settlement is part of a wider push for cleaner water and more accountability from both polluters and public officials:
• In Colorado, regulators now direct payments from pollution violators toward environmental justice needs.
• In Arizona, residents can report local businesses wasting water as drought pressure persists.
• In Alberta, Canada, critics blasted use of tax dollars for a fossil-fuel ad campaign.
• Inditex, Zara's parent company, faced backlash after a concerning operational change increased emissions.
Fights over pollution, water protection, and corporate accountability rarely stay confined to one place. That broader picture helps explain why this PFAS settlement matters beyond a single cleanup effort.
