title: Former classmates reunite as primary school turns 100
content:
Former classmates reunite as primary school turns 100
- Published
It is a school that gave shelter in the devastating Belfast Blitz during World War Two.
And Euston Street Primary School in inner east Belfast is now celebrating its 100th birthday.
It was officially opened in July 1926, just in time to admit pupils for the new school term.
And a century on, the school has opened its doors and classrooms to welcome back many former pupils to celebrate the big birthday.
Among them were Barbara Best and Rosaleen Gilpin, who have been lifelong friends since they met at Euston Street as pupils in the 1940s.
Both, who are now 83, started the school in 1947.
"I started at the same time as Rosaleen, and we've been friends ever since," Barbara told BBC News NI.
Being back in their old classroom triggered many memories, even if things have changed.
"The classroom assistant was a bamboo cane in the corner," Rosaleen said.
"The teachers were strict but they were very good to try and help people from the area to do well."
So was Rosaleen caned at school?
"Well, I've been known to be," she laughed.
For Barbara, the school library was her favourite place.
"You were allowed to go there on a Friday after school, and I remember going down there and thinking 'oh, so many books, great'," she said.
"It was lovely."
And Rosaleen still has a family connection to the school.
Showing her and Barbara round was her granddaughter Sarah McCrossan, who now teaches there.
"It's crazy to think that I'm working in the same place that she came as a child and walked in the same corridors," Sarah said.
"She said that the behaviour management strategies were very different, she said she was sent to the principal's office many times to get the cane which obviously doesn't happen anymore.
"This school is obviously in the middle of a big community and the community is so good to the school and the school is so good to the community."
And in World War Two the school saved many members of that community during the Belfast Blitz.
In April 1941, a German bomb fell on nearby Thorndyke Street, killing many residents including those taking refuge in an air-raid shelter.
So Euston Street Primary's basement became the main air-raid shelter for the local community.
The school sustained damage in a later bombing raid, but the basement kept people safe.
During the anniversary open day, many current and former pupils signed their names on the walls of the historic basement corridors.
Colin Johnston also has a continuing family connection to the school, as his granddaughter Poppy Anderson is a pupil.
Colin attended from 1965 until 1972 and was back being shown round by Poppy.
For him, the technology Poppy uses in school is the biggest difference from his own schooldays.
"All the i-Pads and all that they have now, there was nothing like that in my day," he said.
"It's a big change, it's really modern now."
"I remember my first class down in room five, Miss McConnell, and it was a great school."
He said the school was vital to the local community.
"They cannot do without the school," he said.
"As you see even today, the school dinners and all that and the other things that the school runs it's superb."
And for acting head-teacher Laura Rainey that sense of community was part of the reason for big celebration.
"We've welcomed past pupils, past staff and past governors," she said.
"It's been really lovely just to hear lots of positive memories, happy memories.
"And also some memories that you wouldn't hear nowadays about maybe the cane being used and just how things have changed.
"It's so special to have those stories and that legacy.
"We actually have families that have had four generations come through the school. That says everything."

title: Ubulu-Uku INE Festival: A Celebration of Culture, Peace and Renewal
content:
UBULU-UKU, Delta State — The people of Ubulu-Uku celebrate with gratitude and deep respect His Royal Majesty, Obi Chukwuka Noah Akaeze, and commend his enduring reign and commitment to the growth, peace and development of the ancient kingdom. His support for initiatives that promote the preservation of Ubulu-Uku’s rich cultural heritage remains an important part of the community’s continuing journey.
It was in this spirit of support for the traditional institution and the cultural heritage of Ubulu-Uku that the community came together for the annual INE Festival, in a celebration marked by colour, tradition, unity and, most significantly, peace.
This year’s celebration was particularly remarkable as the festival was held within the palace in an atmosphere free from fighting, violence or disruption. The peaceful gathering represented an important moment for a festival deeply rooted in the history and traditions of the kingdom.
A central figure in the organisation and successful coordination of the celebration was the Traditional Prime Minister of Ubulu-Uku, Chief James Asika Onwordi, the Onishe of Ubulu-Uku, whose vision has consistently centred on fostering progress, unity and growth within the community.
The celebration brought together traditional groups, community stakeholders, youths, families and visitors, creating a vibrant display of the cultural identity of Ubulu-Uku.
Among the major highlights were the traditional displays by the revered Agana men, who performed their sacred rites as part of the festival. The appearance of the Eze Dibia, who had not surfaced publicly for a considerable period, was another notable moment, as he performed his traditional rites to the excitement of those gathered.
The younger generation also embraced the festival with enthusiasm. The major road became a colourful scene of music, dancing and traditional attire, giving the celebration the atmosphere of a cultural carnival while allowing the younger generation to participate actively in the traditions of their forebears.
The presence of major community stakeholders, including the Umuobi, Umu Ozim, Ani-Eke and others, further demonstrated the collective importance of INE to the people of Ubulu-Uku.
The celebration also attracted notable dignitaries, including Rt. Hon. Isaac Anwuzia, Member representing Aniocha South Constituency in the Delta State House of Assembly, Hon. Smart Ijeoma Ufoh, Commissioner for Technical Education, and other distinguished guests.
Beyond the festivities, the INE Festival continues to serve a deeper purpose. It provides an avenue for Ubulu-Uku indigenes at home and in the diaspora to reconnect with their roots, preserve indigenous traditions and strengthen the bonds that hold the community together.
The peaceful conduct of this year’s celebration was particularly significant. It offered a powerful demonstration that culture can be preserved and celebrated in an atmosphere of harmony, mutual respect and communal responsibility.
With the support of the traditional institution and the efforts of those committed to the advancement of the kingdom, the INE Festival continues to provide an opportunity for Ubulu-Uku to celebrate where it has come from while looking towards where it is going.
For Ubulu-Uku, the message from this year’s celebration was clear: culture remains alive, tradition remains relevant, and peace remains essential to the progress and development of the kingdom.

title: Gabriela García narra en fotolibro una crónica familiar marcada por el EZLN
content:
“He estado dividida en dos mundos”, de ahí surge Hay pájaros en el alambre, editado por Hydra
Lunes 7 de septiembre de 2026, p. 5
Gabriela García Rivas, cineasta y narradora visual, tuvo que superar miedos, sacudirse silencios, develar secretos de más de 30 años y aceptar que “he estado dividida en dos mundos”, los cuales dieron forma al fotolibro Hay pájaros en el alambre, tras explorar el archivo fotográfico de sus padres, que participaron en la construcción de un sistema de salud comunitario en Chiapas, antes y después del levantamiento del Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional (EZLN) en 1994.
Desde esa doble mirada, de la pequeña que nació y vivió en esa región a la mujer adulta, decidió “recontar y resignificar su historia”, así como “el vínculo con mis padres (Gabriel García Salyano y Georgina Rivas Bocanegra), la memoria de un territorio en disputa y lo que fui siendo entre esas imágenes”.
La autora puntualizó: “el movimiento zapatista puede contar su historia sin mí, pero yo no puedo contar mi historia sin ese levantamiento” insurgente.
En Hay pájaros en el alambre, desarrollado en el programa Incubadora de Fotolibros 2023, de Hydra –que produce desde la experimentación con narrativas y procesos híbridos–, “se aborda, mediante textos (en español e inglés) e imágenes, una reflexión única y personal acerca del movimiento revolucionario más importante de la segunda mitad del siglo XX en México”, historia de la que la familia de García Rivas es un testimonio vivo.
El fotolibro fue presentado por la autora el sábado pasado en la librería Hydra, donde estuvo acompañada por la fotógrafa y cineasta Maya Goded, así como por Ana Casas Broda, codirectora de Hydra Editorial.
En ese acto se abordó el proceso creativo de García Rivas, se recordó el arduo trabajo de sus padres, se recorrió su trayectoria en distintos formatos y se habló de la superación de sus miedos, así como del derecho de contar una historia, aunque haya pájaros en el alambre.
“Es un libro especial que aborda el zapatismo desde una perspectiva personal y poética; había una narrativa compleja, la cual trabajó Gabriel en la Incubadora sin politizarla; fue increíble, porque las primeras páginas del libro provienen de rollos que fueron revelados 30 años después de que fueron tomados por su papá, y ella los vio por primera vez aquí”, recordó Casas Borda.
Destacó que “ha sido importante la experimentación con materiales y formas de impresión, desde duotono hasta cuatro tintas en offset. En coherencia con la temática del libro, en la producción se experimentó con papeles locales comunes, los cuales tienen diversos usos, que enriquecen la narrativa con diversas texturas, gramajes y pequeñas imperfecciones”.
Maya Goded aseguró: “desde que conocí a Gabriela entendí sus silencios, que aprendió desde chiquita. Ella sentía que su historia no era tan importante por lo grande del movimiento zapatista; sin embargo, reflexionó, sintió y cuestionó. Me emociona que esa niña y su voz, que se mantuvo callada durante tanto tiempo, se quitó los escombros y etiquetas que no dejaban que emergiera”.
En entrevista, Gabriela García, nacida en Chiapas y egresada del Centro de Capacitación Cinematográfica, explicó que la génesis del fotolibro fue la idea de hacer un documental sobre el Islam y su llegada a San Cristóbal de las Casas, justo con el inicio del movimiento zapatista.
“Necesitaba imágenes de la toma de San Cristóbal, el primero de enero de 1994. Entonces pregunté a mi papá, quien había trabajado durante años en las comunidades, si sabía quién podía darme material de archivo. Él, muy quitado de la pena, respondió: ‘allá en el cuarto de las chácharas hay un par de cajas de cartón, chécalas; tomé unas fotos, si te sirven son tuyas’.
“Había un montón de sobres y diapositivas, donde estaba documentado desde el primero de enero y los 15 días siguientes que hubo un cerco militar”. García rescató ese material del polvo y de los hongos causados por el paso del tiempo y se encargó de digitalizarlo.
Al adentrarse en el acervo se dio cuenta de que “además de ese registro, también estaban los procesos comunitarios de capacitación de promotores de la salud y de la construcción, antes y después del zapatismo. Mi padre trabajaba en la zona de Guadalupe Tepeyac, en Las Margaritas; se dedicaba a la formación de promotores de salud, pues había gran mortalidad infantil”.
El peso de los secretos
En esa cotidianidad “crecí con bajo perfil, en silencio, muy en la onda de proteger una vida, la de mi familia y mis afectos. En realidad eran secretos; de repente me di cuenta de que me comenzaban a pesar. Tenía un cuerpo muy aprendido a sobrevivir, enfocado en la vigilancia”.
En la publicación “busco capturar no sólo los momentos significativos de la vida comunitaria, sino también las experiencias y emociones de mi infancia, vivida entre la resistencia y sus silencios”.
El fotolibro presenta material fotográfico de Gabriela García, quien también devela sus propias imágenes, cuyo registro es muy similar a lo que hacían sus padres, pues “trabajo en una organización de parteras tradicionales; documento los procesos organizativos y de aprendizaje”.
García Rivas es narradora visual; su práctica se desplaza entre el cine, la fotografía, la escritura y el trabajo con archivos. En su obra explora las formas de vulnerabilidad social y la relación entre entorno, experiencia individual, memoria e identidad.
Ha dirigido cortometrajes y los ha presentado en festivales nacionales e internacionales. Su ópera prima, El silencio es bienvenido, formó parte de la competencia Premio Mezcal del Festival Internacional de Cine en Guadalajara 2017.

title: Marco temporal, despejo e mineração ameaçam território Pataxó no litoral da Bahia
content: <_cdata>Cerca de 2.000 Pataxó podem perder quase dois terços da Terra Indígena Aldeia Velha em ação movida por empresa agropecuária. Levantamento identificou 34 requerimentos minerários no entorno do território, nenhum deles submetido à consulta da comunidade Pataxó do sul da Bahia protestam contra o marco temporal, tese usada para questionar a demarcação da Terra Indígena Aldeia Velha, homologada pelo presidente Lula em 2024, mas suspensa pelo ministro do STF André Mendonça em 2025 Coletivo de Comunicação da Teia dos Povos Alvos de uma ordem de despejo que pode tirar mais da metade de suas terras, os Pataxó da Terra Indígena (TI) Aldeia Velha, no sul da Bahia, enfrentam uma nova pressão sobre o território: o avanço de projetos de mineração, inclusive de terras raras. A área está cercada por ao menos 34 requerimentos minerários em um raio de 8 km — distância em que a legislação considera a possibilidade de haver impactos sobre áreas indígenas. Metade dos pedidos foi protocolada nos últimos dez anos, segundo dados da ANM (Agência Nacional de Mineração) analisados pela Repórter Brasil. Para lideranças indígenas, a corrida minerária acirra uma disputa de mais de 40 anos entre a comunidade e uma empresa agrícola pela posse da área. “Não era só a especulação imobiliária. É a mineração”, afirma a vice-cacica Ahnã Pataxó. Com 2 mil hectares e aproximadamente 2 mil moradores, a TI Aldeia Velha foi homologada pelo presidente Lula em 2024, mas é alvo de uma ação de reintegração de posse desde 2006, movida pela Cosvar Agropecuária. A empresa reivindica 1.275 hectares da área — quase dois terços da TI. Conhecida como Fazenda Santo Amaro —em referência a um histórico aldeamento indígena no local —, a área foi adquirida pelos fazendeiros em 1983, e registrada dois anos depois em um cartório de Porto Seguro (BA). Contudo, em 1998 os Pataxó retomaram a área, alegando que o local seria de uso tradicional do povo indígena. No mesmo ano teve início o processo de demarcação. Os estudos da Funai, aprovados em 2008, registram a ocupação indígena no local desde o século 16, quando ali existia o aldeamento de Santo Amaro. O documento afirma que famílias Pataxó de várias regiões do litoral sul da Bahia mantiveram vínculos permanentes com a área, utilizada para moradia, agricultura, pesca, caça e coleta. Algumas viveram ali por décadas, enquanto outras frequentavam o território de maneira temporária. A permanência é sustentada, de acordo com a Funai, por documentos, memória oral e vestígios arqueológicos, como antigos locais de moradia, pomares, sambaquis e fornos usados para produzir farinha. Segundo a Funai, a partir das décadas de 1960 e 1970, com a chegada de fazendeiros, muitos Pataxó foram expulsos. Em 1983, quando a Cosvar assumiu a Santo Amaro, havia cerca de 13 famílias indígenas no local. Segundo a Funai, os Pataxó passaram a sofrer ameaças, restrições ao uso da terra e outras formas de pressão para deixarem o local. A maioria das famílias se dispersou pela região, com exceção de uma, a de Dona Dió. O núcleo serviu de base para a organização dos chamados “Pataxó sem terra”. Em 1993, eles fizeram uma primeira tentativa frustrada de retomada da terra. Cinco anos depois, cerca de 40 famílias Pataxó ocuparam a área e fixaram residência. Após a homologação da TI em 2024, a Cosvar recorreu ao STF (Supremo Tribunal Federal) com um mandado de segurança. Relator do caso, o ministro André Mendonça acolheu o pedido da empresa, anulou o decreto de Lula e pediu a reabertura do processo demarcatório. Lideranças indígenas participam de uma das reuniões da câmara de conciliação do STF sobre o marco temporal, coordenada pelo ministro Gilmar Mendes, que foi encerrada em julho de 2025 sem acordo Gustavo Moreno / STF Mendonça entendeu que, como a Cosvar não havia sido indenizada antes da demarcação, a homologação violaria o direito de propriedade. Na decisão, o ministro ignora a presença histórica dos indígenas na área, apontada pela Funai, e destaca que a “ocupação indígena” ocorreu “apenas após a promulgação da Constituição”. Os argumentos de Mendonça fazem referência ao “marco temporal”, tese jurídica segundo a qual os indígenas só teriam direito às terras que ocupavam ou disputavam em outubro de 1988, data de promulgação da Constituição. A regra é criticada por lideranças indígenas e organizações da sociedade civil por ignorar expulsões e outras violências sofridas pelas comunidades. Embora tenha considerado o marco temporal inconstitucional em duas ocasiões, o STF admitiu a possibilidade de indenização pela terra nua a proprietários de boa-fé em algumas situações. O assunto é analisado no julgamento do Tema de repercussão geral 1.031, que ainda não foi finalizado. Foi com base neste processo que Mendonça anulou a homologação da TI Aldeia Velha. A decisão de Mendonça não é definitiva. Ela foi questionada pela Advocacia Geral da União e pela Procuradoria-Geral da República, e os recursos aguardam julgamento do Supremo. Mesmo sem o encerramento do caso, a 1ª Vara Federal de Eunápolis autorizou o despejo. Em julho, no entanto, o ministro Mendonça suspendeu temporariamente a reintegração de posse, até que os recursos sejam julgados. Para a Apib (Articulação dos Povos Indígenas do Brasil), o processo no STF cria um precedente perigoso. “Fazendeiros estão usando o mandado de segurança como instrumento político, para barrar a efetivação dos direitos indígenas. Trata-se de uma ameaça gravíssima, porque homologações presidenciais e processos demarcatórios não podem ser suspensos ou relativizados a favor de disputas pela posse individual da terra”, diz a organização. Assinaura da TI Aldeia Velha pelo presidente Lula ocorreu em abril de 2024, durante a 1ª reunião do CNPI (Conselho Nacional de Políticas Indigenistas), ao lado da ministra dos Povos Indígenas, Sonia Guajajara, e do então ministro da Justiça, Ricardo Lewandowski Divulgação / Ricardo Stuckert/PR A Repórter Brasil procurou a Cosvar Agropecuária por e-mail, telefone e mensagem de aplicativo, mas não obteve retorno até a publicação do texto. Pataxó apontam cerco minerário no entorno da Aldeia Velha Ao se mobilizarem contra o despejo, os Pataxó da TI Aldeia Velha descobriram estar pressionados também pela mineração. A Repórter Brasilteve acesso a uma representação que as lideranças preparam para entregar ao MPF (Ministério Público Federal) e a outros órgãos públicos, na qual identificam dezenas de processos minerários no entorno da terra indígena. No documento, os Pataxó dizem que o processo de reintegração de posse “dissimula operação de cercamento territorial”, a fim de “remover a comunidade indígena para beneficiar exploração de recursos minerais”. Se as extrações minerárias se efetivarem, argumentam, ficarão em uma “bolha isolada”, confinados por um anel de mineração. “Quando chegou essa sentença [de despejo], começamos a querer entender o porquê de a gente incomodar tanto”, relata Ahnã Pataxó, vice-cacica da TI Aldeia Velha. “A gente começou a pesquisar e viu que a mineração está aqui. E a gente ainda disperso no território. Precisou vir isso aí para que a gente percebesse realmente a intenção de nos tirar daqui”, afirma. A Repórter Brasil questionou a Cosvar Agropecuária se a ação de reintegração de posse teria alguma relação com as requisições minerárias, mas não obteve resposta até o fechamento desta matéria. Análise de processos minerários aponta falta de consulta à comunidade indígena A reportagem cruzou dados do Sigmine (Sistema de Informações Geográficas da Mineração) da ANM e identificou 34 requisições minerárias a menos de 8 km da TI Aldeia Velha. O entorno de uma Terra Indígena não é uma área de preservação integral nem de uso proibido, mas tem restrições de uso, de acordo com os atos normativos vigentes da Funai. A Portaria Interministerial 60/2015 considera a possibilidade de impactos ambientais quando atividades de mineração ocorrem a menos de 8 km de terras indígenas fora da Amazônia. Os impactos só são descartados a partir de estudos feitos durante o processo de licenciamento ambiental. Já a Instrução Normativa 2/2015 prevê que o órgão licenciador estadual comunique a Funai quando empreendimentos possam “ocasionar impacto socioambiental direto”. Além disso, a Convenção 169 da OIT (Organização Internacional do Trabalho), ratificada pelo Brasil em 2004, determina a consulta a comunidades tradicionais afetadas por empreendimentos econômicos. Das 34 requisições minerárias no entorno da TI Aldeia Velha, apenas uma está em fase de operação, para exploração de água mineral. Outras 11 estão em fase de licenciamento ou com direito de requerer a lavra (todas para exploração de areia ou argila). As 22 restantes já têm autorização de pesquisa pela ANM, incluindo três de terras raras. Somadas, as áreas cobiçadas pela mineração chegam a 8,6 mil hectares, cerca de quatro vezes o tamanho do território indígena. À Repórter Brasil, a comunidade afirma que só soube agora das requisições minerárias na região e que jamais foi consultada sobre quaisquer destes empreendimentos. “A comunidade indígena de Aldeia Velha nunca teve oportunidade de ser ouvida. A falta de respeito é muito grande e atropela os direitos dos povos originários”, frisa Ahnã Pataxó. Os órgãos estatais confirmaram que não houve qualquer consulta aos Pataxó de Aldeia Velha. Questionado, o Inema, órgão ambiental da Bahia, recomendou que a pergunta fosse feita ao Ibama. O Ibama disse que a competência é da ANM. A ANM, por sua vez, informou que “a legislação vigente não veda a outorga de títulos minerários em áreas contíguas a terras indígenas”. Leia as manifestações na íntegra. Procurada pela reportagem, a Funai recebeu seis e-mails e se comprometeu a responder, mas não o fez até o fechamento deste texto. Ricardo Terena, do setor jurídico da Apib, destaca que “o critério da obrigatoriedade de consulta é o de impacto na comunidade, direto ou indireto”, e acrescenta que na Convenção 169 da OIT “nem se fala de perímetro”. Ele destaca também que “a consulta tem que ser prévia”, o que não aconteceu nestes casos. “Se há requisições minerárias ao redor da TI, já são procedimentos em andamento. A primeira coisa que deveria ser feita, a partir do surgimento destes requerimentos, é a consulta à comunidade”. Uma das preocupações dos Pataxó é em relação à possível contaminação de rios pela exploração de terras raras — conjunto de 17 elementos químicos essenciais à transição energética e às indústrias bélica e de tecnologia. Os três requerimentos na área de influência da TI ocupam 2,1 mil hectares, estando a aproximadamente 500 metros do território e em cima do Rio Buranhém, um dos mais importantes da região. “É nossa fonte de vida”, resume dona Jaçanã Pataxó, pajé da Aldeia Velha. “Os brancos querem tomar as terras indígenas. Os brancos são ricos, não precisam. Será que o coração deles não dói? Acho que deve doer. Porque nesta aldeia os indígenas se criaram, é nosso lugarzinho. Como é que vamos viver?”, questiona dona Jaçanã. “Realmente o céu vai desabar. As pessoas querem cavar a terra para tirar todas as riquezas do solo, destruir história, memória, sustento de um povo sem sequer perguntar”, critica a vice-cacica Ahnã Pataxó, citando os livros “Como adiar o fim do mundo” (Ailton Krenak) e “A queda do céu” (Davi Kopenawa). “Que a população não deixe a responsabilidade para nós e se levante também”, finaliza.

title: At 60, Vietnam's war orphans in US still search for their mothers
content:
Born in Vietnam as Nguyen Thi My Phuong, Murch was one of 150 children who survived the C-5A military aircraft crash during Operation Babylift, the 1975 campaign that evacuated over 3,300 presumed orphans from southern Vietnam to the United States.
As a generation of war orphans, they all left Vietnam when they were too young to make their own decisions. In the minds of many, there remains a constant yearning to fill the memories they "always never had" about where they came from and who gave birth to them.
Time is running out, but the children and many mothers are still waiting to find each other.
In 2005, Murch decided to return to Vietnam for the first time with a group of Babylift adoptees.
She had felt "strangely comfortable."
Unlike others in her group, she was not intimidated by her inability to speak Vietnamese and felt deeply welcomed. For the first time, the American adoptee saw so many people who "looked just like me."
She reunited with pre-1975 orphanage workers to express her gratitude.
"Because of them, we are alive. I printed out a photo taken with them and thought, 'Oh, I am Vietnamese.' That lingered in my mind," she says.
During that trip, she visited the field in District 12 where the C-5A crashed and held a small memorial.
Standing there, she felt more clearly than ever the fragile line between life and death that she and her companions had crossed.
She also returned to Vinh Long Province in the Mekong Delta, where she was born, and visited a local shelter, seeing her own reflection in the eyes of the children there.
However, she did not expect much from her search for her biological family, as there were few clues to offer hope.
Returning to the U.S., questions about her identity weighed more heavily. She did not know exactly where she was taken from or how old she was when she was separated from her mother.
Between her birth in June 1974 and admission to an orphanage in January 1975, intense fighting had swept across the Mekong Delta. No one knew what might have torn a child from their family.
"You realize you don't belong anywhere. I grew up in the United States, but I was born in Vietnam. So what country do I belong to?" she asks.
A series of questions haunted her: If the children are still struggling, can their mothers truly be at peace? A mother separated from her child, whether she chose to let the baby go or for another reason, might have thought about her child her entire life.
In 2024, after talking with a friend battling cancer, Murch realized that surviving the plane crash was a miracle.
"Death cannot take you away, as if you have a superpower and it defies death," the Babylift survivor says.
This inspired her to organize an event in Colorado called "Secret Ability to Fly," honoring those who had cared for, protected and raised the Babylift children. It was the first time she had met other Vietnamese adoptees.
"I realized the desire to be with one's biological family is truly powerful," she says.
At a "War Orphans" gathering in Boulder in March 2024, Murch received a gift: a piece of C-5A insulation material from the very plane that had crashed.
The gift came from Sister Mary Nelle, who worked for Friends For All Children (FFAC) in Saigon from 1972 until April 1975, assisting director Rosemary Taylor.
They received, cared for, and organized the evacuation of orphans. When FFAC closed at the end of the war, all documents, letters, and keepsakes that families had sent with their babies were destroyed.
However, Taylor had recovered the files that survived the destruction, and stored them at the Colorado office along with adoption-related items entrusted to her by others.
After Taylor's death, Nelle took over the collection.
Soon afterward, Murch visited her in a Colorado basement, and the nun handed her a file to look for clues about her identity.
Murch recounts: "I randomly opened the file on top. Miraculously, out of all 33 boxes of documents, my file appeared right before my eyes."
Caregivers at the To Am orphanage had given her the name Mimosa, after the flower.
She found documents detailing the exact day she arrived at the Vinh Long orphanage, her adoptive mother's handwritten letter, crossed-out adoption options leaving only her name, photos from second and third grades, health records, and U.S. immigration adoption updates.
Taylor of FFAC had documented about Mimosa from St. Paul de Chartres Orphanage, Vinh Long, Vietnam.
The child had been issued a birth certificate by a Vinh Long court on Aug. 15, 1974, confirming her status as an orphan with parents unknown.
The child was placed in FFAC's care for adoption on Jan. 15, 1975, and cared for until her departure on April 5, 1975.
Another document from FFAC director Wende S. Grant said: "I hereby certify that Nguyen Thi My Phuong, born on June 24, 1974, in Vinh Long, was surrendered to Friends For All Children for adoption. Her parents have never inquired about her since that day."
Murch says: "For the first time, I saw my name on an official list, on a faded hard copy rather than hearing it through someone else's words. I felt like a missing piece of the past had been put in its right place."
The surprise for her was that, for years, she only knew her Vietnamese name to be Nguyen Thi My Phuong from her adoption registration.
But after seeing the papers Taylor had left, she found that a girl named Tran Ngoc An, born Dec. 28, 1973, who had been raised at St. Paul's Convent in Vinh Long, had also been transferred to the FFAC facility in Saigon on Jan. 15, 1975.
But she did not have a birth certificate, and had been matched with documents bearing the name Nguyen Thi My Phuong.
Murch agonizes: "Am I Phuong or An? That is a missing piece I never knew."
When she was 82, Nelle wanted to find a home for the remaining 33 boxes, hoping they would help connect adoptees searching for their biological families.
"I’ll do it," Murch told her, accepting the responsibility to do something for others like her.
The boxes contained more than just adoption files: There were survivor and casualty lists from the plane crash, convoy manifests of transport companies, flight departure dates, destination addresses, child condition reports post-crash, volunteer lists, personal letters, news articles, film rolls, birth certificates, intake records, and early childhood photos.
Murch says: "These files are a heartbreaking, beautiful, and astonishing testament to war, life and death. They are a piece of my personal history and that of thousands of other adoptees."
She began sorting, categorizing, cross-referencing, and transcribing the records of Babylift children evacuated in April 1975.
One day, she suddenly realized that if it was so important to her, someone who had not even been searching for her past, what could it mean to others?
As if by destiny, Murch had been entrusted with a project to preserve thousands of records and documents from the wartime child-welfare organization.
She joined the Society of American Archivists.
She is now learning about cataloging, data management, descriptive formatting, risk management, privacy protection, and regulations for personal documents.
By organizing, digitizing, and indexing this collection, she hopes to preserve it for future generations.
Finding her biological parents brought healing to Huyen Friedlander, the last child placed aboard the final flight of Operation Babylift.
Following a trip to Vietnam in 1996, she became a therapist specializing in trauma, grief, and loss.
In graduate school, she focused her research on transracial adoption.
She says: "Most people do not understand the inner world of adoptees. These were the same painful experiences happening inside me before I found my mother."
Based on attachment theory, she says caregivers are the first to mirror a child's sense of self through interaction. For Friedlander, all her caregivers abruptly vanished in April 1975.
"I didn't know who I was anymore. That was deeply traumatic, even though I couldn't articulate it at the time."
A 2000 study by Ohio State University involving 169 Vietnamese war adoptees across 10 U.S. cities highlighted similar struggles. While 76% wanted to meet their biological fathers upon arriving in the U.S., only 30% knew their fathers' names. About 22% attempted contact, and only 3% succeeded.
Born to American military personnel and Vietnamese civilians, most of these children never knew their fathers' names or addresses.
Often, they possessed only a faded photograph or stories passed down from their mothers.
The cross-continental flights effectively closed the door on the past for many, particularly those aged four to nine. Initially fluent in Vietnamese, they lost their mother tongue entirely.
When Friedlander first arrived in the U.S., she could still sing a Vietnamese song.
She later realized that her cultural detachment was the result of severe psychological trauma.
Now in her 50s, Friedlander looks at photos from her early days in America and sees a profoundly traumatized, dissociated child avoiding eye contact with strangers. A psychological wall separated her past from her present, shielding her from the deep pain of her losses while allowing her to feel safe in a new life.
Despite having a loving adoptive family, she had felt isolated growing up mixed-race in the U.S. Surrounded by taller peers, having a different skin color, and facing discrimination at school, she constantly felt inadequate.
"When my biological mother left me at four, my true self died. I became a compliant child, seeking safety, fearing conflict, and terrified of displeasing people because I feared rejection. I lost myself," Friedlander says.
Within the roughly two weeks between leaving Vietnam and meeting her adoptive family, she lost everything familiar: her mother, relatives, home, language, food, and culture.
Later, when she visited Little Saigon in California, people spoke to her in Vietnamese. Unable to understand, she felt a heavy burden of guilt when asked why she could not speak her native language.
Working with hundreds of adoptees, Friedlander observes parallel traumas. Many share a collective pain of feeling unloved, rejected, or believing they had caused something terrible.
Common struggles include identity crises, self-rejection, racism, isolation, difficulty assimilating, feelings of inferiority, and body image issues.
For Friedlander, reclaiming control of her life meant reconnecting with her homeland.
In September 2025, she and a group of Babylift adoptees cycled through the Mekong Delta. Most were still searching for their biological mothers.
During a rest stop in Can Tho, 52-year-old group member Le My Huong suggested an idea: actively approaching Vietnamese families to find their mothers.
Adopted in Australia and surviving an abusive childhood, Le had endured her own traumatic search. She was kidnapped as a child and deceived for 47 years by her captor, who claimed to be her biological mother.
When she returned to Vietnam in 2004, she met with a family that falsely claimed her as theirs. It took 14 years for the truth to be known.
She says: "I was completely broken. Fortunately, I eventually found my real mother. That was the healing. After decades of living a lie, I am still learning how to carry the weight of the truth."
Over the past two decades, Le has helped many adoptees return to Vietnam to search for their families after being struck by the realization that the answers usually lie within the community and not in adoption paperwork.
Because most documents contain false information, many adoptees do not even know if their recorded names are real.
Le concluded that the only reliable way to find biological families is through DNA testing and cross-referencing global genetic databases.
The group agreed.
Friedlander, Le, Era Goodland, and Jane Joy went on to co-found Mother Search, a non-profit facilitating family reunions through DNA matching.
Launched in September 2025, Mother Search seeks to connect searching children and parents by sharing photos and information. Participants receive free DNA testing kits, which normally cost upwards of $50.
The samples are uploaded to major European and American databases, such as MyHeritage, which holds around 9 million profiles, and Ancestry, which has over 30 million, to increase the matching potential.
So far, five pairs of relatives have been matched and three reunifications involving two adoptees in France and one in the U.S. have been facilitated.
"If it weren't for DNA matching, they would never have found each other because all their paperwork was wrong," Le says.
Rather than rely on one-to-one matches, the project aims to expand the pool of DNA profiles from overseas adoptees while simultaneously collecting samples from mothers in Vietnam.
She notes that a Vietnamese family recently sent her a photo of an 83-year-old mother who is still searching for her long-lost son. Seeing the profound sadness in her face reaffirmed the urgency of their work.
"Mothers and children are still waiting to be found."
The organization believes that reconnecting with roots is essential for adoptees to reclaim their identities after an immeasurable loss. It hopes governments will eventually facilitate widespread, affordable, and accessible DNA testing.
"If state agencies in both Vietnam and the U.S. provided easily accessible archival information, it would help heal the wounds caused by this separation," Friedlander says.
Murch is pursuing the same goal.
Her questions and the 33 boxes of newly discovered files brought her back to Vietnam for a second time in May 2026. She visited national archives, locating thousands of documents related to wartime adoptions. At the end of her journey, she returned to Vinh Long simply to sit in quiet reflection in her birthplace.
She ruminates: "I know the chances of finding any clues are very slim, and I don't expect much. I just went there to walk around and reflect on what my life in 2026 would look like if I hadn't left Vietnam in the final days of the war."
Deep down, she still yearns for the memories she never had. For adoptees like her, discovering their origins is a form of validation.
Using the Friends For All Children archives, Murch and her colleagues are now tracking down Babylift adoptees across the U.S. to hand-deliver their personal files.
She says: "Witnessing history appear like a miracle, seeing your own name in the legacy of war, is incredibly important. A tiny piece of truth means everything to someone who knows nothing."
She says there are many other individual adoption cases beyond the records she has collected, highlighting the need for a central archive to consolidate records from various sources and help women find their children easier.
"I hope the governments of both countries can establish an agency to support the children of the war.
"And we need a compassionate community so that the complex legacy of the war isn't treated merely as a personal problem for those born at the intersection of history."
As the youngest victims of the conflict, these former orphans are still searching for an answer to the question that has vexed them for nearly six decades: Who am I?
Story by Hong Phuc, Kim Hoa

title: Good News in History, September 18
content:
188 years ago today, the Anti-Corn Law League was established in England by the economics-savvy liberals who understood that protectionism is immoral and useless in benefiting the economy. The League, led by Richard Cobden and heavily influenced by economist Daniel Riccardo, succeeded in seeing the Corn Laws of 1815 abolished, laying out the first laizzez-faire arguments against mercantilism to be heard in Europe, and establishing for all time the case study on their use. READ more about this successful political movement… (1838)
The Corn Laws imposed tariffs on imported cereals into England under the guise of protecting the domestic production (corn meant any grain at the time). As in all economic activity, the Corn Law tariffs had two effects, which renowned French economic journalist Friedrich Bastiat described famously as one which is seen, and one which is unseen.
The tax on imported wheat meant that producers of the more expensive domestic cereals were able to keep their jobs and production methods intact—a perceived good by the British Parliament.
That which was unseen was manifold. They resulted in a rise in the price of bread at a time when British factory owners were trying to reduce costs. It resulted in food scarcity among the poor as bakers and merchants could no longer import cheaper grains from abroad even in times of shortages. It stalled English farmers from further agricultural innovations, or moving into other industries, having a portion of their income all but guaranteed.
It also decreased the demand on manufactured goods, as suddenly the lower and middle classes were paying more for food they had gotten for less prior to the Corn Laws’ enactment. Lastly, as organizer Cobden saw it, it created unnecessary animosity between nations who might otherwise live in greater harmony if trade were partaken freely.
The lessons of the Corn Law were never lost to history, but rather must be reiterated every time a political administration attempts to re-establish protectionism and mercantilism according to naive desires of obtaining that good which is seen: the protection of a domestic market, and ignoring that which is unseen—the burden imposed on the rest of the economy in exchange.
MORE Good News on this Day in history:
- George Washington laid the first cornerstone of the Capitol building (1793)
- Tiffany & Co. was founded in New York City (1837)
- Daniel David Palmer administered the first chiropractic adjustment (1895)
- The Columbia Phonograph Broadcasting System made its broadcasting debut through its network of over 16 radio stations— later it took the name CBS (1927)
- President Reagan announced the destruction of nuclear warheads by US and USSR (1987)
- Ted Turner, the innovative founder of the first cable news network (CNN), donated 1 billion dollars to the UN, to create the United Nations Foundation, a charity that works to help the world’s poor and preserve the environment (1997)
75 years ago today, A Streetcar Named Desire, the film based on the play by Tennessee Williams, premiered in New York City. Starring Vivien Leigh, Marlon Brando, Kim Hunter, and Karl Malden, the film tells the story of a Mississippi southern belle, Blanche DuBois, who, after encountering a series of personal losses, seeks refuge with her sister and brother-in-law in a dilapidated New Orleans apartment building.
Tennessee Williams collaborated with Oscar Saul and Elia Kazan on the screenplay. It received Oscar nominations in 10 other categories (including Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay), and won Best Supporting Actor (Malden), Best Supporting Actress (Hunter), and Best Art Direction (Richard Day, George James Hopkins), making it the first film to win in three of the acting categories.
In 1999, A Streetcar Named Desire was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress as being “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant”.
In his 2020 autobiography Apropos of Nothing, director Woody Allen praises every aspect of the production. “The movie Streetcar is for me total artistic perfection… It’s the most perfect confluence of script, performance, and direction I’ve ever seen,” he wrote. (1951)
156 years ago today, a party of explorers from the Washburn-Langford-Doane Expedition traveled down the Firehole River and entered the Upper Geyser Basin, where they found an extraordinary natural feature they would call “Old Faithful“. Nathaniel P. Langford, the expedition leader wrote in his journal of the day’s discovery, noting “it spouted at regular intervals nine times during our stay, the columns of boiling water being thrown from ninety to one hundred and twenty-five feet at each discharge, which lasted from fifteen to twenty minutes. We gave it the name ‘Old Faithful.'”
First things first, the regular intervals at which it discharges are due to it being separated from all the “plumbing” of the Upper Geyer Basin’s features. Intervals between eruptions can range from 60 to 110 minutes, averaging 66.5 minutes in 1939, and slowly increasing to an average of 90 minutes apart today due in theory to earthquakes altering the subterranean water table or other features.
In the early days of Yellowstone National Park, Old Faithful was often used as a laundry, with one employee writing… “Old Faithful is sometimes degraded by being made a laundry. Garments placed in the crater during quiescence are ejected thoroughly washed when the eruption takes place. Gen. Sheridan’s men, in 1882, found that linen and cotton fabrics were uninjured by the action of the water, but woolen clothes were torn to shreds.” (1870)
And, 78 years ago today, Margaret Chase Smith became the first woman elected to the US Senate. For more than three decades, she served as a role model for women aspiring to national politics; she was also the first woman elected to the US House of Representatives and the first to have her name placed in nomination for the US Presidency of a major party.
Senator Smith bravely denounced the Communist witch hunt of McCarthyism at a time when others feared that speaking out would ruin their careers. On June 1, 1950, she delivered her courageous 15-minute “Declaration of Conscience” speech, defending every American’s “right to criticize…right to hold unpopular beliefs…right to protest.”
Breaking their paralysis of fear, six other moderate Senate Republicans signed onto her Declaration. She said McCarthyism had “debased“ the Senate to “the level of a forum of hate and character assassination… with the four horseman of… fear, ignorance, bigotry, and smear,” and Republicans had hurled unproved charges with reckless abandon.
[From her speech] “I think that it is high time that we remembered that the Constitution, as amended, speaks not only of the freedom of speech but also of trial by jury instead of trial by accusation. Whether it be a criminal prosecution in court or a character prosecution in the Senate, there is little practical distinction when the life of a person has been ruined… The exercise of these rights should not cost one single American citizen his reputation or his right to a livelihood nor should he be in danger of losing his reputation or livelihood merely because he happens to know someone who holds unpopular beliefs.” (1948)
16 years ago today, 42-year-old Frenchman Philippe Croizon became the first quadruple amputee to swim across the English Channel. He trained for years, hoping to demonstrate the abilities of handicapped people, and finished the swim in under 14 hours. With the aid of paddle-like prosthetics attached to the stumps of his legs, the French swimmer completed his dream of swimming between five continents two years later. (20 10)
80 years ago today, Tonka Trucks was founded. First called Mound Metalcraft, they opened in a metal manufacturing plant in Mound, Minnesota. The three businessmen, Lynn Everett Baker, Avery Crounse, and Alvin Tesch changed their company’s name to Tonka Toys in 1955, using the Dakota Sioux word “Tanka” or Tonka, which means “great” or “big”.
The logo at this time was an oval, showing the Tonka Toys name in red above waves, honoring the nearby Lake Minnetonka.
A Museum in Winifred, Montana has collected more than 3,000 of the metal trucks, bulldozers, cranes, graders, and all varieties of construction vehicles.
The slogan ‘Tonka tough, built to last’ has been proven true as the steel toys are handed down from one generation to the next—and still holding up. (1946)
And, 176 years ago today, Harriet Tubman fled the plantation where she was enslaved, escaping to freedom in Philadelphia. Traveling at night so she would not be seen by slave catchers, she followed the North Star that guided her 90 miles toward the Mason-Dixon line. Once passing over that border from Maryland into Pennsylvania, she would be free.
The first person to help her was a white woman who was a Quaker. She sheltered her the first night and gave her instructions on where to go next. Tubman is quoted in a biography, as saying, “When I found I had crossed that line, I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees and over the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaven.”
Born into slavery, the five-foot woman named Araminta (‘Minty’) Ross grew to be strong and determined. She earned extra cash for her escape by working even longer than she was required to on the Poplar Neck Plantation in Dorchester County, Maryland. Because all her family and friends were still enslaved, she subsequently undertook 13 perilous missions back to the state to bring more than 70 people to freedom and help them find work…
Having changed her name to Harriet Tubman, she traveled in extreme secrecy, staying with members of the Underground Railroad—to which the original Quaker woman belonged. The network provided safe houses and transportation for fugitive slaves. Tubman (who came to be known as ‘Moses’) “never lost a passenger.”
During the American Civil War, she served as an armed scout and spy for the Union Army, advising officers on how best to attack the South. In her later years, Tubman was an activist, with her friend Susan B. Anthony, in the struggle for women’s suffrage, and established schools that would educate freedmen in South Carolina. After her death at age 90 or 91, she was buried in a ceremony with full military honors. (1849)
