En 2017, Vigo-Trauco puso en marcha una misión de rescate muy poco habitual, y fue gracias a esa estrategia que dio con el polluelo al que le dio el nombre de Parker.
Su objetivo era reclutar parejas de guacamayos rojos silvestres para que actuaran como padres adoptivos de las crías condenadas.
Al convencer a las aves silvestres de asumir esta tarea, esperaba probar una nueva vía de salvación para las crías desatendidas de Perú, y para la especie en su conjunto.
¿Por qué las guacamayas rojas descuidan a sus polluelos más pequeños?
Es imposible no ver a las guacamayas rojas. Su plumaje carmesí resalta sobre el verde del bosque, y sus graznidos se escuchan mucho antes de verlas.
Cada hembra puede poner hasta cuatro huevos por temporada, pero por lo general solo una o dos crías llegan a volar fuera del nido.
"Los padres, y en particular la madre, dejaban de lado [al más pequeño]", afirma Vigo-Trauco, codirectora de The Macaw Society, una organización peruana de conservación que reveló este comportamiento tras instalar cámaras en los nidos en 2007.
"El polluelo pasa frío y grita; cuando llega el padre, alimenta a la madre y a las [primeras y segundas] crías, pero deja al tercero gritando".
No se observó acoso entre hermanos ni que estuviera relacionado con la disponibilidad de alimentos en el área. Entonces, ¿por qué descuidan los padres a sus crías más pequeñas?
Vigo-Trauco opina que a los padres les resulta difícil atender a crías que se encuentran en etapas de desarrollo distintas. Incluso una diferencia de cuatro o cinco días en la eclosión puede ser determinante, porque los polluelos necesitan regímenes de alimentación, hasta temperaturas de nido, muy distintas.
Los padres se ven obligados a elegir, explica. Si se esfuerzan demasiado por alimentarlos a todos, corren el riesgo de que ninguno sobreviva.
Cómo ayudan los padres de acogida de animales silvestres
Para las poblaciones relativamente saludables de guacamayas rojas de la Amazonía peruana, la pérdida de los polluelos más jóvenes tiene menos repercusiones.
Pero en países donde los conservacionistas pelean en contra de cazadores furtivos y madereros por la supervivencia de cada ave, Vigo-Trauco dice que la muerte de así sea un puñado de polluelos es un desastre.
Criar a mano a los polluelos rechazados es una solución posible.
Sin embargo, pueden pasar entre un mes y medio y tres meses hasta que puedan emprender el vuelo.
Además, los loros criados en cautividad tienen tasas de supervivencia notoriamente bajas: les cuesta alimentarse en libertad, identificar a los depredadores y formar bandadas.
Por eso es que el equipo de Vigo-Trauco recurrió a la idea de usar padres adoptivos silvestres.
Después de capturar a Parker en 2018, el equipo de Vigo-Trauco lo alimentó a mano en su estación de campo durante tres semanas, siguiendo un horario riguroso de intervalos de dos horas.
Igualmente, examinaron los nidos del bosque para encontrarle al polluelo una familia adoptiva adecuada que le enseñara a desenvolverse como un ave silvestre.
Esta técnica había sido probada anteriormente por avicultores que criaban guacamayas en cautividad —entorno donde las condiciones están controladas y el intercambio de nidos implica simplemente cruzar un pasillo con el polluelo—, y también se basa en experimentos realizados con otras aves silvestres, como las cotorras hombroamarillo en Venezuela durante la década de 1990.
Finalmente, el 22 de diciembre se puso a Parker en un nido nuevo y su madre adoptiva, Tambo, empezó a acicalarlo de inmediato.
Pocos meses después, pudo emprender el vuelo. Fue apenas el cuarto polluelo en conseguirlo después de décadas de observaciones de nidos silvestres en Tambopata.
El equipo obtuvo resultados parecidos con otros 25 polluelos rescatados entre 2017 y 2019.
Otros tres fueron adoptados con éxito, pero no lograron independizarse (ya que murieron a causa de un rayo, un depredador y una enfermedad).
Ya en 2019, Vigo-Trauco se sentía más segura: "Me sentía como si estuviera jugando ajedrez: moviéndome de un lado a otro para ver qué era posible".
Las deficiencias del sistema de acogida
Aunque la crianza en condiciones silvestres facilita el avance, trae consigo muchos desafíos.
Es una labor costosa.
Durante su experimento de tres años en Tambopata, Vigo-Trauco pudo contar con fondos suficientes para cubrir los salarios, el alojamiento y el equipo de un equipo de 20 personas.
Pero dice que que una iniciativa así de ambiciosa "no es fácil de replicar".
Además, es una tarea difícil de llevar a cabo.
Rony García-Anleu es director de investigación biológica de la Wildlife Conservation Society en Guatemala.
Fue pionero en la implementación del método de adopción en las últimas poblaciones de guacamaya roja que quedan en el país y coautor del artículo de Vigo-Trauco sobre la crianza por padres adoptivos.
Sin embargo, la última vez que el equipo de García-Anleu introdujo un ave en un nido de acogida en Guatemala fue en 2019.
La crianza por padres adoptivos en estado silvestre requiere de una sincronización perfecta, según cuenta.
Es necesario adentrarse kilómetros en la selva para localizar un nido con un polluelo en peligro y, después, encontrar una pareja con un nido adecuado que esté vacío o uno que contenga un polluelo de edad parecida.
En cambio, su equipo les enseña a las guacamayas a volar, a alimentarse y a establecer vínculos sociales dentro de una jaula de grandes dimensiones, para después liberarlas cuando están listas.
Volando hacia adelante
A pesar de sus defectos, la técnica de crianza en libertad está sirviendo de base para el trabajo con otras especies de loros, desde Argentina hasta Centroamérica, señala Vigo-Trauco.
Además, desde 2020 ha estado probando una variante: prescindir por completo de la fase de crianza a mano y trasladar los polluelos de un nido a otro tan pronto como nacen.
Este nuevo enfoque exige un mayor seguimiento, pero necesita menos cuidados intensivos para los recién nacidos, lo que reduce los costos operativos.
De igual manera, ya ha dado resultados positivos en el segundo año del proyecto: se logró intercambiar con éxito los polluelos de dos nidos —cada uno con dos crías de edades muy dispares— para que los padres pudieran criar a dos polluelos de edad similar.
Vigo-Trauco cree que esto podría abrir la puerta a fomentar esta práctica en lugares con menos recursos.
"Es gratificante ver que nuestra población, relativamente más sana, nos permitió convertirnos en una fuente de conocimiento para otros", afirma Vigo-Trauco.
En cuanto a Parker, logró dejar el nido y alzar el vuelo.
El equipo de Vigo-Trauco volvió a verlo en septiembre de 2019; ya era un guacamayo joven y seguro de sí mismo que volaba junto a sus padres adoptivos y su hermano.

title: Mariscal Cáceres: concurso del Pescado Pango se realizó en fiesta por Virgen de la Merced
content:
17:39 | San Martín, set. 20.



Con el colorido y el bullicio propios de las celebraciones patronales, se dio inicio oficial a las festividades en honor a la Virgen de la Merced, patrona de la provincia de Mariscal Cáceres, región San Martín. Una de las actividades más esperadas por la población local fue el tradicional concurso costumbrista del Pescado Pango, que año tras año congrega a un numeroso público en torno a una de las expresiones más genuinas de la identidad cultural de la zona.


El certamen, que se ha convertido en un emblema de las fiestas mercedinas, puso a prueba la rapidez, destreza manual y el conocimiento práctico de las participantes en una dinámica tan sencilla en apariencia como exigente en su ejecución: pelar plátanos y retirar las escamas de pescados propios de la zona en el menor tiempo posible.
Bajo la atenta mirada del jurado y entre el aliento constante de familiares, amigos y curiosos, cada concursante desplegó técnicas transmitidas de generación en generación, en una suerte de homenaje viviente a las labores cotidianas que durante décadas han definido la vida ribereña de la provincia.
Tras varios minutos de intensa competencia, resultó ganadora la participante que logró completar ambas tareas —el pelado del plátano y el descamado del pescado— en el tiempo más corto, sin que ello fuera en desmedro de la calidad del trabajo realizado, uno de los criterios que el jurado tuvo en cuenta al momento de definir a la vencedora. Su triunfo fue celebrado con aplausos y vítores por el público asistente, que no dejó de acompañar cada etapa del concurso con entusiasmo.
La actividad fue organizada e impulsada por el Sindicato de Trabajadores de la Municipalidad Provincial de Mariscal Cáceres, entidad que, a través de esta y otras iniciativas similares, busca contribuir a la revaloración y preservación de las costumbres locales.
Según los organizadores, el propósito central de este tipo de concursos es generar espacios en los que las tradiciones puedan ser conocidas, practicadas y, sobre todo, transmitidas a las nuevas generaciones, de modo que el vínculo entre la población y su patrimonio cultural inmaterial no se debilite con el paso del tiempo.
El concurso costumbrista del Pescado Pango se enmarca dentro de un calendario más amplio de actividades programadas con motivo de las festividades de la Virgen de la Merced, celebraciones que combinan la fe religiosa con expresiones culturales, gastronómicas y recreativas propias de la provincia.
En esta ocasión, el evento sirvió como punto de encuentro para la población, que además de disfrutar de la competencia, tuvo la oportunidad de compartir un ambiente de confraternidad en torno a la celebración de su identidad.
Con esta primera actividad, la Municipalidad Provincial de Mariscal Cáceres y las organizaciones locales dan inicio formal a una agenda festiva que se extenderá en los próximos días, y que continuará reuniendo a los pobladores en torno a la devoción mariana y a la reafirmación de las tradiciones que distinguen a esta provincia sanmartinense.

title: Meet the chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
content:
Meet the New York City chefs who kept Ground Zero workers fueled after the 9/11 attacks
Members of "Operation Chefs With Spirit" reflect on the tragedy 25 years later.
Chef Don Pintabona spent years cooking up the finest dishes for celebrities, Wall Street brokers and other VIPs at the Tribeca Grill in downtown Manhattan, but nothing could have prepared him and the rest of the city's restaurant community for their biggest job.
In the hours after the World Trade Center was attacked and destroyed on Sept. 11, 2001, Pintabona said he and many other chefs, caters, food service workers and others all yearned to help the city in some capacity with their skills, but didn't immediately know how.
But through quick thinking, organizing and the generosity of thousands New Yorkers, Pintabona and the other restaurant members put together a massive operation that fed Ground Zero workers around the clock for two months after the attacks.
"Everybody kind of just said, 'Okay, let's jump in,'" Pintabona, 66, told ABC News.
He and other volunteers of "Operation Chefs with Spirit" said that even though 25 years have passed since the attacks, the memories of those weeks are still fresh, as is the sense of awe at how they put the operation together.
Turning the page on a tragedy
Pintabona said he had a desire to do something after the attacks to help the city, but it was a little piece of paper that came to him serendipitously that sparked his idea for the operation.
On Sept. 11, he said he watched the destruction of the towers from the roof of his home in Brooklyn, which was so close that pieces of paper debris from the towers were floating in the air near him.
One of those was a "P" page from a dictionary and when Pintabona picked it up he said he noticed that one side of the page had words with negative connotations, such as pesky, while the other side had words such as persevere, perseverance, persistence.
“9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
"I mean, in my mind, this came straight from heaven, that through the perversion, you gotta persist, you gotta persevere," he said. "So those words were banging around my head for the days and weeks and just trying to figure out how can I live up to this."
Pintabona said the next day he was able to get to his restaurant, and he started cooking with what he had in his kitchen. He then brought the food to Stuyvesant High School in lower Manhattan, which was one of the staging areas for first responders.
"We had just floods of people coming in to attack the food," he said adding that the meals were gone in a matter of hours.
Pintabona said he wanted to continue to feed more people but transporting the meals through the streets, which were damaged and restricted to first responders and the National Guard, would be a challenge. He said he had a eureka moment during a cigarette break while watching the Hudson River.
"I saw a barge…And I said, 'Holy s---, this is it. We've got to feed everybody by boat,'" he recalled.
A crew assembles, quickly gets into action
Pintabona told ABC News he found that that other chefs in the city were also interested in feeding the Ground Zero workers and they all put their heads together.
He soon started calling up several contacts within the food industry, the city government and the owner of Spirit Cruises, which operated city sightseeing and party cruises lines, and things quickly began to fall in place.
Spirit provided three boats, one at Chelsea Piers that would be used to cook and prepare the meals, another to transport the food to Ground Zero, and a third, a triple decker, stationed in Battery Park City near the pit that was used for the workers to eat and rest.
The city's top chefs, such as Charlie Palmer, Danny Meyer and Daniel Boulud, and food workers and volunteers would be doled out with tasks with everything from cutting veggies to organizing forks, spoons and plates.
Jim Stewart, a longtime food service coordinator who had experience coordinating food operations at the Meadowlands and other big clients, jumped in when Pintabona made the calls for help. Stewart said he too was compelled to do something after the attacks.
"I think at that point, having something to do was sort of helpful, and it gave you some sort of purpose in a very difficult situation," Stewart, 66, a Navy veteran, told ABC News.
Stewart used his connections to secure food from the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, which was still in fridges following the end of that year's U.S. Open.
Stewart and Pintabona estimated that the food from the tennis center could serve 75,000 meals, but that was all eaten within three days.
Fortunately, they weren't the only New Yorkers who were willing to share from their fridges. Stewart recalled how a whole slew of Downtown Manhattan restaurant staff, from small Chinatown restaurants to larger, more elite eateries like the ones under B.R. Guest, were calling him up and ready to offer their food.
"So they would be bringing down enormous amounts of food packages to go. All the cooks from down there, they brought meals for like 200 people without question for a month," Stewart said.
"I would get a call, and they would go, 'At the airport, there's two pallets of beef from Texas.' It was not just New York," Stewart added.
Pintabona said that thousands of New Yorkers arrived at Chelsea Piers ready to volunteer, even those who never cooked a meal in their life.
Although Pintabona had to turn many would-be volunteers away because of space and logistics issues, he said he worked out to tailor their skills to fit the operation.
"When they would come on, I would try to talk to as many as possible. 'Okay, you work at Smith Barney in the accounting department? You know what? We need you to help us inventory the food that comes in off the trucks,'" he recalled. "A lot of people, obviously servers and whatnot, food service people, I would put them front-facing on the buffets, you know what they're used to."
Megan Murphy was a full time bartender at Rue 51 in Manhattan on Sept. 11 and she told ABC News she immediately answered Stewart's call. She helped to serve the food and coordinate with other volunteers right at the pit.
"It was my call to duty," Murphy, 51, told ABC News while holding back tears. " I had been doing something because I was helpless. I felt helpless and I just wanted to help. I just want to be…I just needed to be there."
'Nourishing more than their stomachs'
By Sept. 14, the operation had kicked off and the volunteers were ready to go and the first set of food was delivered to the pit.
The boats would sail from Chelsea Piers nearly 2 1/2 miles south to Ground Zero with a team of volunteers and return back for another round and the operation would continue 24/7.
Workers still had soot on them and looked liked they hadn't slept in days but they gladly accepted the meals and cherished the time to step away from the terrible scene.
Pintabona said massage therapists joined in on the volunteering and provided the crews with free massages to ease their muscles.
He said the meals definitely helped the pit workers have the energy to push through with their work, but the chefs and volunteers all felt that their service meant a lot more than a free lunch.
"You'd see the looks on the faces of people that came in, if they'd been on the pile for God knows how many hours and starving and then they got to sit in a clean environment and then talk to other first responders," he said.
"So that was the most amazing part of the effort," he added, "[It] kind of nourished a lot more than just stomachs."
Murphy, who continued to bartend at night during her volunteer time, said that many who came down to help went beyond just serving food and in many cases offered the pit crews a place to unwind and let out their raw emotions.
"I would make an effort just to go to everyone and talk to them, and let them talk to me about the experience," she said.
"If after lunch they could walk out and I could walk out with them and they were smiling and getting off their shift and made it a better day, that was what I was there to do," Murphy added.
The volunteers and chefs said that while they pushed forward with the operation, with some sleeping on the boats, the stress and hard work did compound.
Fortunately, the volunteers had each other's backs, according to Pintabona and Stewart.
"It got so ridiculous that one day Jimmy was working the phones and, you know I just had this stupid, selfish craving for a Krispy Kreme doughnut," Pintabona recalled.
"I said, 'All right, let's call this guy.' We called them, and the next day a whole truck with like 20 rolling racks of Krispy Kreme donuts showed up," Stewart said. "So [Pintabona] looked at me and was like, I should have known better."
Looking back 25 years later
The operation ended after roughly two months and roughly a million meals after the Red Cross came in and took care of meals for the Ground Zero pit crew. But Pintabona said that the crew didn't grow apart.
He organized a Christmas party at Cipriani in Soho for all of the volunteers and their families and many stayed in touch in the last 25 years.
Stewart said he was humbled by the outpouring of support from not only New Yorkers, but people throughout the world who heard about the feeding operation and were moved.
"I have these pictures that were sent to me from a class where the children, they drew cartoons," he recalled. "They said like, 'Keep going. You're doing great.' You know, 'thank you for your efforts.'"
Murphy said that she is still emotional thinking back to the weeks after the attacks, but the memories of selfless New Yorkers always stand out.
"New York is strong, New Yorkers are strong," she said.
Pintabona agreed and said for him it all came back to that floating dictionary page and that push to persevere.
"You have to turn the page and stay on the positive side. So that's kind of what I've learned through this experience," he said.

title: Assam teacher teaches tech to moms, won nat'l award
content:
Under this programme, called "Each One Teach One," students walk their mothers through UPI payments, online banking, using smartphones and basic reading. Bordoloi started the initiative two years ago after noticing a growing gap between his tech-savvy students and their mothers, many of whom had little or no formal schooling and struggled with even basic technology, the Times of India reported.
A daily lesson at home
For Bordoloi, the idea was simple: rather than confining digital literacy to the school gate, make children the ones carrying it home. "When a child becomes a teacher at home, education becomes a shared journey," he told the Times of India. "There is something deeply inspiring about seeing a student sit beside his or her mother and patiently explain how to use a mobile phone or make a digital payment."
Nine out of ten students in the programme belong to the agriculture-dependent Mising tribal community, spread across Majuli and nearby areas, per the report. What began in Kalbari has since spread to five more villages: Banhphala, Bhekelichapori, Dhankhuli, Laliti Chapori Gaon and Sarigharia.
For many of the mothers, the lessons are about more than convenience. Learning from their own children has become a source of motivation to keep sending their kids to school, since the arrangement gives the household a direct, visible return on education.
School backs the effort
The school has built on the programme by using government-provided smart boards during parent-teacher meetings to demonstrate digital tools directly to mothers. Principal Rajib Kumar Baruah said the initiative had helped many women overcome their hesitation around technology, the Times of India reported.
Bordoloi's community work extends beyond digital literacy. For several years, he has also campaigned against child marriage, an effort that began in Bhekelichapori, where minor girls would routinely drop out of school and elope.
Credit shared with the community
Bordoloi is one of 48 educators across the country to receive the National Teachers' Award this year. He was quick to deflect individual credit for the recognition. "This award is for my school, colleagues, students, parents and the community," he said, as per the Times of India report.
The programme's growth from a single village to six, entirely through word of mouth and visible results at home, has been cited as a model for how schools in similar tribal and rural settings could address adult literacy without requiring large government interventions. For now, in the villages around Kalbari, the daily routine remains unchanged: children come home from school not just with homework, but with a lesson plan for their mothers.

title: JEP resolvió la situación jurídica de más de mil comparecientes
content:
La Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (JEP) ya ha resuelto unas 1.030 renuncias a la persecución penal. En términos más simples, son casos de comparecientes que no fueron considerados máximos responsables de crímenes durante el conflicto y cuya situación jurídica ya quedó definida.
La medida hace parte de la Ruta No Sancionatoria, que está a cargo de la Sala de Definición de Situaciones Jurídicas. Esa ruta se ocupa de los comparecientes que estuvieron involucrados en crímenes, pero no tuvieron un papel determinante en su planeación o ejecución.
“Es por esta vía entonces que los familiares de las víctimas del conflicto armado pueden acceder a respuestas sobre el cómo, cuándo y dónde ocurrieron los hechos”, dijo el presidente del tribunal de paz, Alejandro Ramelli.
En su intervención el presidente de la JEP, magistrado Alejandro Ramelli Arteaga, habló sobre el significado que tiene para las víctimas encontrarse con los comparecientes que no son máximos responsables en la Ruta No Sancionatoria:
— Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz (@JEP_Colombia) September 9, 2026
“Para las víctimas, este proceso ha… pic.twitter.com/Lls4jpG5Ex
El 95% de los beneficiarios son de la Fuerza Pública. De las 1.030 decisiones, 979 fueron para sus integrantes. Otras 46 fueron para comparecientes de las extintas Farc y las cinco restantes, para agentes del Estado, civiles colaboradores y un tercero civil.
La medida se concretó en 43 resoluciones entre 2024 y 2026. Son decisiones definitivas que cierran la situación jurídica de los comparecientes.
- En la práctica, borran sus antecedentes penales y extinguen las sanciones disciplinarias, administrativas o fiscales relacionadas con los hechos.
- Los comparecientes cobijados estuvieron involucrados en 377 hechos que dejaron 643 víctimas directas en distintos departamentos.
- Entre ellos están Antioquia, Boyacá, Casanare, Caquetá, Cesar, Córdoba, Cundinamarca, Huila, Meta, Norte de Santander y Santander.
¿Por qué importa? Porque para las víctimas y sus familias, que un caso termine por esta vía no significa simplemente que el compareciente quede libre de responsabilidad. La renuncia a la persecución penal viene con compromisos como contar la verdad, ayudar a buscar y entregar dignamente a las víctimas y hacer actos de reparación simbólica.
Además, como varios de ellos estuvieron involucrados directamente en los crímenes, pueden aportar detalles importantes sobre lo que pasó.
Un ejemplo es el famoso abrazo que ocurrió en esta Sala entre el compareciente Andrés Rosero y la mamá y la hija de John Darío Giraldo Quintero, asesinado y presentado como guerrillero muerto en combate por integrantes del Batallón de Artillería No. 4 “Jorge Eduardo Sánchez”.
“Este es un momento que necesitábamos para poder sanar”, aseguraron en su momento.

title: Stitching the Future: Technology as a Sacred Trust
content:
Stitching the Future: Technology as a Sacred Trust
By grounding our digital strategy in the same values as our ancestors, we can ensure technology serves our school community rather than consuming it.
September 9, 2026
Paul McKinnon / Shutterstock
In an era where artificial intelligence promises to archive human culture at the touch of a button, Indigenous communities face a vital question: Who has the right to own, shape and digitize sacred knowledge?
Long before AI became a headline in education, this question fundamentally reshaped my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. But understanding how to protect our community’s digital future didn’t start in a computer lab; it began in a quiet valley in Wisconsin, with my grandmother’s unfinished quilt and a ribbon skirt workshop that changed everything I knew about knowledge itself.
I grew up in a small rural village tucked into Wisconsin’s Driftless Area, where winding roads disappear between steep bluffs and deep valleys, and every hill seems to reveal another breathtaking view. It was a place shaped not by glaciers, but by time. A landscape as rugged as it was beautiful.
It was also home to my grandmother — a strong cheesemaker’s wife who was, in some ways, the quintessential grandmother figure. She hosted Sunday family dinners, baked fresh bread, volunteered at the local food pantry and quilted with the other ladies from church twice a week. She also cursed like a sailor and wasn’t stingy with her love or hugs.
In my teen years, she became my shelter — a quiet refuge from a chaotic home and a reminder that love exists even in the hardest seasons. When I went away to college, she sent me away with a quilt made just for me, a special gift we all only receive once. As an adult, she became the reason we visited the Driftless Area and was the glue that kept our families together. During that time, she showed that love to my children, who adored her.
After a long stay in a nursing home and years of declining health, my grandmother passed away last year. After her passing, my twin sister and I discovered her last unfinished quilt tucked away in a forgotten storage bin. Her hands hadn’t been able to hold the material or work the sewing machine for a long time, and we thought all the quilts had been claimed. Finding one more, even unfinished, felt like a blessing.
Around the same time, my twin sister and I both signed up for a staff ribbon skirt class where members of the Indigenous community would teach us not only how to make ribbon skirts, but also share teachings about how to wear them respectfully and as true allies. Carrying pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt with us, we set out to create ribbon skirts in her honor.
Before that class, I knew very little about ribbon skirts beyond seeing them worn at school celebrations and community events. I quickly learned they are not tied to a single tribe, but are worn by Indigenous women across many Nations, each with their own traditions, teachings and stories. I also learned that a ribbon skirt is much more than a beautiful piece of clothing. It represents identity, resilience, and the enduring strength of Indigenous women.
Today, communities across North America celebrate Ribbon Skirt Day each January, recognizing not only the skirts themselves, but the right of Indigenous people to wear them with pride after generations of policies that sought to erase their cultures.
What surprised me most was that our class wasn’t really about making skirts. It was about learning the responsibility that comes with them. We learned when it was appropriate to wear a ribbon skirt, what it meant to wear one as an ally, and why those teachings mattered as much as the sewing itself. Anyone can buy a ribbon skirt online, but creating one alongside community members who generously shared their knowledge transformed it into something entirely different. Every stitch became part of a relationship built on trust, respect and a willingness to learn.
That experience changed the way I thought about knowledge itself. I realized that some things are valuable not because they can be owned, bought, or preserved, but because they carry stories, relationships and responsibilities that extend far beyond any one individual. They belong to the communities that shaped them and to the generations who will inherit them.
The tension between owning knowledge and stewarding it sits at the very heart of my work as the instructional technology coordinator at Indian Community School. If knowledge is built on trust and community relationships, then technology cannot simply be an instrument to extract, scale, or monetize data. That conviction was tested in 2021, well before generative AI became a household conversation, when a company approached our language and culture department with an extraordinary proposal.
They offered innovation. A way to immortalize language and culture through “virtual ancestors” — artificial intelligence trained on the stories, voices, and wisdom of living tribal elders. As the instructional technology coordinator, I was initially excited about what an extraordinary opportunity it would be to place our school at the forefront of modern technology!
However, the more my colleagues and I analyzed the pitch, the more our excitement gave way to deep alarm. The offer was riddled with deep red flags: vague promises around intellectual property, zero accountability for data privacy and a predatory push to extract sacred community knowledge. But recognizing those red flags was only half the battle.
Facing a tool this complex also exposed the gaps in my own understanding of artificial intelligence at the time. I realized that properly vetting this proposal and ensuring our school’s technology program moved forward in a good, grounded way required more than just caution. It demanded that I build my own AI literacy so I could stand as an informed guardian for our community’s data.
That 2021 proposal became the catalyst for a journey that has defined my work ever since. Recognizing gaps in my own understanding, I immersed myself in AI literacy, digital ethics and Indigenous data sovereignty frameworks. As we start the 2026-27 school year, AI is no longer a distant possibility; it is actively shaping how stories are told, how knowledge is created and how data is harvested.
In response, my role has evolved from simply managing technology infrastructure to helping our school build an ethical digital sanctuary. We began facilitating professional development sessions that empower our teachers to critically evaluate AI tools through a lens of cultural safety and data privacy. In the classroom, we reaffirmed our dedication to active digital stewardship over passive consumption.
Rather than allowing third-party algorithms to dictate or summarize Native experiences, our students now engage in hands-on digital storytelling, learning how to protect their personal and cultural data while using modern tools to amplify their authentic voices on their own terms.
The core lesson I learned in that ribbon skirt class remains my guiding principle: technology, like knowledge, is only as valuable as the relationships and trust behind it. For educators, leaders, and communities navigating this fast-shifting landscape, maintaining agency over our stories requires asking hard questions before we ever sign a contract or adopt a tool:
- Who owns the data being used to train this system? In my school, we actively reject software platforms that do not explicitly provide full intellectual property rights to the school.
- Does this tool respect the sovereignty and living culture of the community it serves? I work with stakeholders to ensure that software and platforms do not train on student or staff data, and I prioritize tools with the least environmental impact.
- Are we adopting technology to enhance human relationships, or replace them? We prioritize tools that bring elders, teachers and students together in real-world dialogue, using technology as a bridge for connection rather than a substitute for human presence.
When my sister and I stitched pieces of our grandmother’s unfinished quilt into our ribbon skirts, we weren’t just preserving her memory; we were continuing a relationship rooted in love, honor and continuity. That is the true essence of stewardship. When we approach technological innovation not as a rush to extract the future, but as a solemn duty to protect what was handed down to us, we ensure that modern tools honor where we came from. In the age of AI, our responsibility remains unchanged: to stitch technology into the living fabric of our communities in a good way, ensuring our stories remain whole, authentic and undeniably our own.

title: Kushe Aunshi honours fathers, keeps ancestral traditions alive

Kushe Aunshi honours fathers, keeps ancestral traditions alive
Devotees across Nepal marked the Hindu festival with offerings to their fathers and rituals to remember departed ancestors.Deepak KC
Hindu devotees across Nepal observed Kushe Aunshi on Friday, honouring their fathers and paying tribute to deceased ancestors.
The festival is traditionally marked by children offering their fathers their favourite foods and expressing love, respect and gratitude.
Those whose fathers have died gathered at sacred sites to perform rituals including shraddha, tarpan and pindadan. At Gokarneshwar Mahadev Temple in north-eastern Kathmandu, popularly known as Uttar Gaya, devotees performed the rites on the banks of the Bagmati river.
Large numbers of devotees also visited the Pashupatinath Temple and other religious sites across the country.
Also known as Gokarne Aunshi, the day holds a dual significance in Hindu tradition, celebrating the bond between children and their fathers while providing an occasion to remember and honour departed family members.
Kushe Aunsi falls on the new moon day of the Nepali month of Bhadra. The day is also associated with the collection of kush, a sacred grass used in Hindu rituals throughout the year.

title: La historia de Maggie Walker, la hija de esclavos que se convirtió en la primera mujer en fundar un banco
content: La mujer también dirigió durante décadas una sociedad que ofrecía seguros y apoyo económico a la comunidad negra en época de segregaciónNo todos la conocen, pero fue la primera mujer desarrolladora de videojuegos: la historia de Carol Shaw En 1901, ante el consejo de la Orden Independiente de San Lucas, una mujer afroamericana de 37 años se puso de pie y anunció lo que, a ojos de todo el mundo, parecía un disparate. Quería crear un banco, un periódico y unos grandes almacenes gestionados por y para la comunidad negra de Richmond, en Virginia. Cinco años después, los tres proyectos eran una realidad y la mujer, que se llamaba Maggie Lena Walker, había hecho historia en Estados Unidos. Conseguir lo que consiguió era impensable para una mujer como ella en un momento como aquel, marcado por la segregación entre negros y blancos. “No nací con una cuchara de plata en la boca, sino prácticamente con una cesta de ropa sucia sobre la cabeza”, llegó a decir la protagonista de esta historia sobre sus primeros años de juventud. Hoy recordamos su historia. Maggie L. Walker nació el 15 de julio de 1864 en Richmond, hija de Elizabeth Draper, una mujer que había sido esclavizada, y de Eccles Cuthbert, un periodista de ascendencia irlandesa. Poco después de su nacimiento, su madre se casó con William Mitchell, mayordomo en la misma casa en la que ella trabajaba. La familia consiguió cierta estabilidad económica hasta que un día Mitchell apareció ahogado en el río, algo que obligó a la madre de Maggie a buscar nuevas formas de ganar dinero. Decidieron abrir una lavandería en casa, donde la joven Maggie empezó a trabajar repartiendo ropa limpia entre clientes blancos. Estudió, trabajó y consiguió su objetivo Walker pudo estudiar en las primeras escuelas públicas para afroamericanos de Richmond y se graduó como maestra en 1883. Ejerció durante tres años, hasta que se casó con Armstead Walker Jr. en 1886 y tuvo que renunciar, ya que no estaba permitido contratar a mujeres casadas. Apartada de la docencia, decidió dedicar su vida a la Orden Independiente de San Lucas, una sociedad afroamericana que ofrecía diferentes ayudas a la comunidad. Walker fue escalando puestos durante casi dos décadas hasta que, en 1899, la organización, al borde de la quiebra, la nombró Gran Secretaria, cargo que ocuparía hasta su muerte en 1934. Fue ya en este puesto cuando puso en marcha su ambicioso plan: el periódico St. Luke Herald (1902), el banco Saint Luke Penny Savings (1903) y el Saint Luke Emporium, unos grandes almacenes con empleados negros (1905). El banco fue el proyecto que más perduró y Walker lo concibió como una herramienta de independencia económica para una comunidad a la que los blancos solían negar los préstamos. “Juntemos nuestro dinero, usemos nuestro dinero, invirtámoslo entre nosotros y cosechemos el beneficio nosotros mismos… Tengamos un banco que tome los centavos y los convierta en dólares”, dijo para anunciar el proyecto. A lo largo de su historia, el banco fundado por Maggie Walker benefició a cientos de personas en Richmond. Para 1920, la entidad había otorgado más de 600 hipotecas a familias negras, permitiendo a muchas cumplir el sueño de tener una vivienda propia.

title: Raghubir Yadav ran away from home after failing class 12, earned Rs 2.50 a day: ‘Slept hungry’

Raghubir Yadav ran away from home after failing class 12, earned Rs 2.50 a day: ‘Slept hungry’
Raghubir Yadav recalls running away from home after his Class 12 failure, joining theatre and earning Rs 2.50 a day while often going hungry.
Long before Raghubir Yadav became one of Hindi cinema’s most recognisable character actors, his introduction to the performing arts came through the travelling world of Parsi theatre. Raghubir was associated with Bhopal Theatre, which was run by Madanlal Kapoor, the father of actor Annu Kapoor and Seema Kapoor. Recalling that period, Yadav said he lived a ‘nomadic’ life, travelling from one place to another performing plays, earning just Rs 2.50 a day and sometimes going to bed hungry, but said those years became an important part of his learning.
Raghubir Yadav ran away from home
In a conversation with Hindi Rush, Raghubir Yadav said he left home after finding out that he was going to fail his Class 12 examinations. Embarrassed and unsure about what to do next, he left with a friend and reached Lalitpur, where Bhopal Theatre was performing.
“I had run away from my home because I found out I was going to fail my 12th grade. I was embarrassed. I ran away with a friend. We reached Lalitpur, where Babu Ji’s theatre company, Bhopal Theatre, was performing. I watched a play called Nagin there.”
However, his friend soon left him, leaving Yadav behind in Lalitpur.
“After a few days, my friend left me. So, I ended up at Babu Ji’s theatre company and met him. He asked me what I did, and I told him I sang songs. He asked me to sing something, and I sang a ghazal.”
Raghubir Yadav then recalled how Madanlal Kapoor spotted his potential but also pointed out a major weakness in his singing.
The actor said, “Babu Ji said, ‘You sing very melodiously, but your talaffuz (pronunciation) is very poor.’ I thought maybe it had something to do with the tabla and told him that if I could sing with a tabla, I’d improve my talaffuz. Everyone started laughing. He said, ‘No, it’s your pronunciation that needs work.’ He took me under his wing, and with his guidance, I learned Urdu and improved my pronunciation.”
Raghubir Yadav spent six years travelling with theatre troupe
Raghubir Yadav soon began travelling with the theatre troupe, spending the next six years living a nomadic life as the company performed across different parts of North and Central India.
“I was associated with Parsi theatre, so for six years I lived a nomadic kind of life. We travelled everywhere — Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan. We went to every place, village after village, and performed theatre.”
The actor said the experience was less about earning money and more about learning. He recalled that the performers had very little to spend on food and basic necessities.
“We never really thought about our stomachs. It was almost like an education. We had our books, and life simply went on. I used to get Rs 2.50 a day, but when it rained, we had to manage with Rs 1 or Rs 1.50.”

‘We would eat half the roti and save the other half for the night’
Raghubir Yadav went on to describe how he and the other theatre artistes managed their meals during their travels.
The actor said, “We would buy flour for four annas and tomatoes for four annas and make chutney. We would borrow a tawa from someone’s house, make a stove under a tree and cook rotis. We would eat half and save the other half for the night.”
There were also days when they had nothing to eat.
“Many times, we would go to sleep hungry in the evening. But even while being hungry, we kept laughing. Annu, Guddo (Seema Kapoor) — we were all together. We actually enjoyed even that hunger.”
Yadav also remembered the atmosphere created by the Kapoor family, saying music, books and practice were a regular part of their lives.
He said, “That was the atmosphere we enjoyed. There were books. Mummy would always say, ‘Don’t sit idle.’ There was music practice going on all the time. Songs were always playing around us. We kept getting opportunities to learn.”
Raghubir Yadav recalls Annu Kapoor teaching him a song
Raghubir Yadav also shared an anecdote about Annu Kapoor teaching him a song during his days with the theatre company. Yadav said Annu had told him the song, prompting him to learn and perform it.
“Annu had taught me a song — ‘Reshma jawan ho gai, teer kamaan ho gai.’ I learnt it from him and sang it. I got beaten up for that.”
Annu Kapoor’s mother, whom Yadav affectionately refers to as “Mummy Ji,” was standing near the stage with a pair of tongs to beat him for singing the song.
“She was standing beside the stage with a pair of tongs. It was a very cultured, disciplined kind of atmosphere,” he said.
‘A person always learns through deprivation’
Raghubir Yadav said he looks back at those years fondly and considers deprivation an important part of his education.
“A person always learns through deprivation. There were so many shortcomings. We weren’t getting enough food; we were hungry. But even today, those were some of the most beautiful days of my life.”
He said he and Seema still talk about that period.
“Even today, when we talk about those days, Seema says, ‘Bhaiya, those were such beautiful days.’ Sometimes, remembering them makes us cry.”
Yadav added, “Those were tears of joy — the happiness we felt then, the way we looked at learning and the hard work we had to put in. There was a different kind of pleasure in all of it. I am thankful to the Almighty that He kept us in deprivation, because a person learns through deprivation.”
Raghubir Yadav’s career
After his years with the theatre company, Raghubir Yadav studied at the National School of Drama (NSD) in Delhi and later joined its Repertory Company. He made his film debut with Massey Sahib (1985).
Over the years, Yadav has delivered acclaimed performances in films including Salaam Bombay!, Lagaan, Peepli Live, Newton and Sui Dhaaga.
On television, he became widely known for playing Brij Bhushan Dubey in Mungerilal Ke Haseen Sapne and later won a new generation of viewers as Pradhanji in Panchayat.

title: Shityuwete state funeral row: Family questions hero criteria
content:
The shityuwete family has questioned the government’s decision to bury liberation struggle veteran Helao Shityuwete at Gammams Cemetery instead of Heroes’ Acre.
The family yesterday at the funeral asked the government to tell them what requirement their ‘tatekulu’ [uncle] did not meet to have accorded him a state funeral at Heroes’ Acre.
“Why was a man with such an extraordinary, undeniable liberation record not accorded a national hero’s funeral and buried at Heroes’ Acre? What requirement did he not meet?” family spokesperson Julius Ngweda asked.
Presidential spokesperson Jonas Mbambo is yet to respond to questions on the matter.
Shityuwete died on 29 August a few days after he turned 92.
He leaves Betuel Nuunyango as the only surviving member of the group of 37 Namibian nationalists who were imprisoned on Robben Island during the 1960s.
Ngweda on Friday said Shiytuwete had told the family that he wished to be buried next to his comrades, Andimba Toivo ya Toivo and Dimo Hamaambo.
His fellow prisoners, following the announcement of the state funeral on Thursday, described it as an insult to a man who spent 18 years on Robben Island fighting for a better Namibia.
Ngweda yesterday said Shityuwete had since 1998 requested that his fellow comrades, such as Eliaser Tuhadeleni, Immanuel Shifidi and Nathaniel Maxuilili be brought back from Robben Island, expressing appreciation to the government for honouring his wish.
“But as a family, we want answers. His record speaks for itself. He endured imprisonment and sacrificed precious years of his life for a free Namibia,” Ngweda said yesterday.
He said the future generation deserves to understand how the sacrifices of liberation heroes are assessed and honoured.
“We are grateful for the state funeral, but history must be properly acknowledged. We hope the question will be considered with the dignity and seriousness that Tatekulu deserves,” he said.
Ngweda expressed gratitude to the former prisoners for consistently checking up on Shityuwete.
“Friendship and commitment did not end when time became difficult. You remained present and demonstrated that the bonds forged during the struggle for freedom are bonds that can be endured for a lifetime,” he said.
“Today, we stand on the shoulders of people like him. His presence brought people together and we should not let his departure become the end of this history,” he said.
Former anti-apartheid activist and political prisoner Jerry Ekandjo on Saturday said Shityuwete is a hero and that the former fellow prisoners want an answer from the government.
Namibian Former Robben Island Prisoners Trust chairperson Marten Kapewasha at the occasion said: “What can we do? We will just accept.”
Shityuwete was a firm labour advocate, fighting for the rights of all workers in the country and for the dignity of all. He started the Namibian Former Robben Island Prisoners Trust to take care of former Robben Island prisoners and their families.
Shityuwete walked to Tanganyika, now Tanzania, and back to Namibia in 1965 to start a liberation front in the country.
Many remember him as a fearless freedom fighter and a humble man who remained committed to freedom, equality and humanity.
Former prime minister Nahas Angula described him as a man of perseverance.

title: Adaptive yeast form of 'scientific empathy' for tempe makers: Ministry
content:
"This yeast research, which uses native Indonesian Rhizopus mold, is not just a biological breakthrough, but a form of scientific empathy for tempe makers' concerns," the Ministry's Science and Technology Dissemination and Utilization Director, Yudi Darma, said here on Friday.
He made the statement during a public discussion titled "Nusantara Yeast: From a Piece of Tempe for Food Security" at the Antara Heritage Center (AHC) on Wednesday (September 2).
He explained that yeast plays an important role in making tempe, which has become an inseparable part of Indonesian society.
"Tempeh is not merely a filling food. It is a Nusantara masterpiece representing noble character and cross-generational survival. Its history runs deep, including in the Serat Centhini (1815), where tempe symbolized hospitality, harmony, and nutritional sufficiency for Javanese society," he said.
However, he added, tempe was once looked down on during the colonial era as a lower-class food. That stigma collapsed in 1965, when Prof. Ko Swan Djien of Bandung Institute of Technology (ITB) opened the world's eyes through tempe fermentation research with US collaborators.
The global medical and nutrition community has since recognized tempeh as a superfood, a superior plant-based protein source rich in immune-boosting antioxidants, cholesterol-lowering properties, and a mainstay for nutritional rehabilitation of children with chronic digestive disorders.
The UI research team, through the Bestari Saintek Program funded by the Indonesia Endowment Fund for Education (LPDP), developed a tempe yeast innovation combining several Rhizopus species.
Bestari Saintek researcher and UI academic Prof. Wellyzar Sjamsuridzal said the yeast research was part of efforts to understand and preserve Indonesia's microbial biodiversity.
"Tempe yeast is an important part of efforts to utilize Indonesia's biodiversity to strengthen food security. Through research and collaboration, microorganism diversity can be responsibly developed into innovations that benefit society," he said.
