title: The Boge-Bada arrives at Era Kone
content:
The Boge-Bada arrives at Era Kone at around 1 pm, welcomed by traditional dancers from Manumanu Island and the Tabu dancing group from the Hanuabada village.
The traditional Hiri Lakatoi is the centrepiece of the annual Hiri Moale Festival in Port Moresby, celebrating the historic trade voyages of the Motu people.
Looking back to the history of the Lakatoi, the first Lakatoi was built by Edai Siabo, from the village of Boera.
According to the legends told, Edai Siabo was returning from a fishing trip when a great eel appeared and dragged him under the water. The eel was believed to be the spirit of the sea.
He returned Edai to the surface of the sea, after instructing him to build a great Lakatoi, to fill it with cooking pots, and to sail westward, following the south-east trade wind called the laurabada in the Motu language.
Obeying the spirit, he built the first Hiri-Lakatoi, named it Bogebada (which means sea-eagle), and had it loaded with pots made by his wife.
He and his friends then sailed up the coast into the waters of the Gulf of Papua. That is where the historical Hiri-Trade Voyage was formed, which is now an important part of the culture of the Motu people.
For months, the Bogebada and its crew were away. The villagers were all convinced the crew had perished. They mocked Edai’s wife and tried to force her to remarry.
Before Edai left, he had instructed her to stay within a corner of her house, not to bathe in the sea, to keep a tally of the days the Bogebada had been gone, to keep her fire burning, and to have her skin tattooed by an old woman.
Failing to stick to this routine would endanger the expedition and the lives of Edai and his men.
One day, a Lakatoi appeared on the horizon and slowly approached the village. It was Bogebada.
Edai was arriving back home, a hero. His wife jumped into the sea and washed away her accumulated dirt, put on her finest costume, walked out onto the verandah of the house, hit it with a stick, shouted, Hedihoroha Bogebada and began dancing in joy.
The traditional Hiri voyages carried the much-prized Motu cooking pots to the people of the Gulf of Papua and brought back plentiful supplies of sago for the Motu.
For the Motu people, along the coast, the land and the sea provided what sustained their families and community. Food was life, food was wealth, food was a symbol of generosity and togetherness.

title: The Boruca Peoples’ Non-Linear Path to Self-Determination: Defined by Community Resilience
content: The Boruca Peoples’ Non-Linear Path to Self-Determination: Defined by Community Resilience Country Costa Rica agnes Tue, 09/08/2026 - 09:11 Issues Human Rights Program 5 Main Image By Iza Harris The Boruca Peoples have faced immense imposition from outsiders since the Spanish conquest in the 1500s, spanning from colonialism to the current governance structure under the Democratic Republic of Costa Rica. Costa Rica became an independent state in 1838, though Indigenous communities there did not receive legal recognition until 1977 and did not gain the right to vote until 1994. Despite some legal progress toward recognizing the need for self-determination and representation of Indigenous Peoples, the federal government has essentially carried the torch of the conquistadors. Currently, governance operates through Integral Development Associations (ADIs), local governing bodies intended to represent each Indigenous territory. Within Boruca communities, the ADIs have encouraged passivity—a stark contrast from the communal ethos that has long been central to Boruca life. Carlos Morales Lázaro (Boruca), a former ADI vice president, says that the government’s failure to implement legal procedures to protect Indigenous Peoples’ rights and defense against invading Peoples is “proof of institutionalist racism, a relic of colonialism... which presents this country as an ecologist’s paradise to the outside world while failing to seriously protect ethnic groups who follow a model of ecologically sound agricultural practices.” Brún̈cajc community leader José Ángel says that before the installation of the ADI, both designated Boruca territories (Rey Curré and Boruca Village) were governed by an active citizenry who were keen to work on communal projects and mutual aid and devoted to raising future leaders. The majority of Borucan community members agree there has been a retreat from community engagement as power became concentrated within the development organization. In Boruca Village, there was a time when various committees would work in tandem. When public streets and spaces needed cleaning, for example, the town would get together in the hundreds and do their share. It was more than just working together to solve problems; it was a time of celebration and joy in shared spaces. “We had more autonomy before today, [whether] there were problems or times of celebration. It was a communal decision where different committees worked together,” Ángel affirms. The day before we spoke, Ángel recalls that heavy rains nearly washed the village’s bridge away. Before the ADI, everyone would have been energized to resolve the issue, to bring shovels and machetes and cut down nearby trees to fix the problem. Now, he says, “the municipality’s machinery comes, it gets fixed. And if not, no one helps.” The sense of responsibility to participate in civil services has been snuffed out by bureaucracy, while the disconnect between organizations has grown. Now, each enterprise within the territory receives funding that must be accounted for and solely distributed toward the needs of each individual organization—an approach that inhibits cross-collaboration and resolution of issues. “This type of regulation killed the form of organization that the town had,” Ángel says. Ángel’s comments reflect the sense that laws and regulations applied to the Indigenous territory are “closing us off,” reducing community participation to individuals doing their day jobs and returning home without an interest in further resolution of issues. Years ago, he worked as a teacher in the local reservation school. At that time, he says, teachers had the power and influence to teach the importance of communal thinking and action within the classroom. Now, however, a culture of passivity has infiltrated the schools, and teachers are no longer personally invested in creating future leaders in their students. “If they were to train leaders [today],” Ángel says, “they would be leaders who are just looking around to see what they can grab, how they can benefit from being there.” The underlying sentiment of Ángel’s comments is that imposed governmental structures have usurped the sense of communal responsibility, heightening individualistic, self-serving, and financial motivations of people throughout the governing body and town. As a result, people are less willing to participate in projects without compensation. The Indigenous collectivist mindset has been eroded by the disease of the capitalistic mindset, which has been imposed on these Indigenous territories. Despite the growing distance between governance and community, there are still occasions where the Boruca Peoples are exercising communal identity and the power exerted within it. One such example is the community’s fierce fight against the development of the Diquís Dam, a project proposed by the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE), a state-owned utility. The project was initially proposed in the 1970s, then redesigned and publicly launched in the mid-2000s, designed to be the largest dam in Central America. It would have had a catastrophic impact on terrestrial and marine ecosystems, causing flooding and disruption to the Boruca community in Rey Curré. The fight against the installation of the hydroelectric dam was waged by Maria Lázaro’s activist grandfather, Don Christiano Lázaro. In a 2024 article in "Terralingua," she detailed the beginning of the fight: “In 1978, the Peoples of Ujarrás, Salitre, Cabagra, Térraba, Boruca, and Yímba Cájc took over the civic center of Buenos Aires canton as a form of protest and rejection of the project.” This mass mobilization of people included Indigenous leaders, community members, and various organizations who refused to be the victims of a massive imposition on their lands. The original project was projected to “displace 1,600 persons, including 500 Indigenous people.” Rafael González. Artisan and Elder Rafael González was one of the community members opposing the project; he participated in the various peaceful marches to Buenos Aires and La Merced Park in San Jose to the Legislative Assembly and the Presidential Palace. González spoke of the various community groups that spearheaded the resistance to the megaproject, such as the Mujeres con Espíritu de Lucha, or Women with a Fighting Spirit, as well as other men’s groups. He remarks that this $2.5 billion project would have only harmed local communities while lining the pockets of national institutions and international contractors. “The greed for money that comes along...that’s what spreads. Good ideas, good deeds are thrown in the trash,” he says. There was plenty of back-and-forth regarding the legality of the project. In 2011, the Constitutional Court determined that it was constitutional “as long as the Indigenous communities were consulted within a period of six months from the notification of the ruling.” Yet, no consultation was conducted, and therefore, the condition necessary to proceed was not met. The Indigenous communities involved were not interested in the offers made to relocate them in exchange for well-paying jobs. Speaking for the community, beloved Terriba martyr Jehry Rivera, now deceased, said, “We don’t believe in the promises of employment for Indigenous Peoples, as up until today it had been demonstrated that all the qualified and best paid personnel have been brought from the outside. Indigenous workers are used only to break rocks.” The community’s fight was aided by the ADI, which filed a lawsuit against ICE, forcing workers off their land. The lawsuit corroborated that a consultation process never took place. Eventually, the fight was won, and in 2018, the project was indefinitely halted. The dynamics at play show the strength of the Boruca in their conflicts with neighboring Indigenous communities. The ADI played a role, yet was not the utmost factor of importance in pushing for the rights legally granted to Indigenous Peoples within their territories. Leaders throughout the Boruca community hope that in the future, Boruca youth will be trained to be invested in their community and traditions. Morales Lázaro notes how vital it is that the Boruca Peoples find ways to maintain their identity and to critically reflect on the imposed and adopted forms of education taught to their children. “We must not forget that [imposed] education tells us that learning happens within four walls. But the Indigenous way of life has always been to learn by observing, by example,” he says. “Young people need to be trained, and more importantly, to gain experience” in local organizing and communal activity, so that “when we older people aren’t here anymore, they will continue the defense of rights.” Maria, who is young and community-oriented, is frustrated with the lack of involvement of her Boruca peers in the fight for their human rights and representation. Her approach is to follow in the footsteps of her justice-seeking, community organizer grandfather, and to join her peers across Salire, Terriba, and other Indigenous communities. She acknowledges that the objective of the state government is to divide so Indigenous people don’t see their collective needs, because “all their fights are connected.” Fortunately, having inherited her grandfather’s temperament and sense of duty, she is carrying the torch for the shared struggle of a resilient and culturally vibrant community. -Iza Harris is a recent graduate from Pitzer College with a Bachelor of Arts in International Political Economy whose work centers on justice, indigeneity, and decolonial perspectives as pathways toward a more environmentally conscious, caring, and equitable society. During her time at Pitzer, she studied abroad in Nepal and Costa Rica, conducting in-depth research with the Raute and Boruca Indigenous communities to uplift the voices and perspectives of communities whose experiences are often unheard or dismissed.

title: Tajikistan’s Practices in Combating Land Degradation Have Attracted the Interest of the International Community
content:
As part of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (COP-17) in Ulaanbaatar, Tajikistan’s practices were presented as examples of sustainable land management. Among them are the creation of stone terraces on mountain slopes, methods for soil and moisture conservation, as well as the use of sunken greenhouses.
Stone terraces: protecting slopes from erosion
One of the most well-known practices has been terracing of mountain slopes.
On steep rocky areas, special stone terraces are created. They help retain soil, slow down water movement along slopes, preserve moisture, and reduce the risk of destructive mudslide processes.
Such structures make it possible to use previously unsuitable land for agriculture and grow fruit and fodder crops on them. For mountainous Tajikistan, this is particularly important since arable land is limited.
Sunken greenhouses: heat preservation and food security
Among Tajikistan’s practices, the report separately highlights sunken greenhouses.
Such greenhouses are partially located below ground level, which helps retain heat. Stones inside the structure are used as natural heat accumulators.
This technology makes it possible to grow vegetables and other crops even during the cold season and helps rural families provide themselves with food year-round. The distinctive feature of this practice is that it was developed with the participation of women from rural areas.
Leadership in the international WOCAT database
Tajikistan also stands out for the number of registered practices in the international WOCAT database (World Overview of Conservation Approaches and Technologies), which collects solutions for sustainable land management.
According to the report, the country has documented 124 technologies and 57 approaches related to land conservation. This is one of the highest indicators in Central Asia.
The database includes various solutions that are applied in mountainous regions: soil and water conservation methods, restoration of degraded areas, approaches to sustainable use of agricultural land.
Forest and vegetation restoration
Another direction in combating land degradation is the restoration of forests and vegetation.
According to the report’s data, the forest area in Central Asia has increased by 6.4% in recent years. Among the region’s countries, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan are named as leaders: in Tajikistan, the growth of forest territories is estimated at 23%.
Forest plantations help strengthen soil, reduce erosion risk, retain moisture, and increase ecosystem resilience to climate change.
Transition from addressing consequences to land restoration
The authors of the regional report note that Central Asian countries are gradually transitioning from responding to the consequences of degradation to systematic land restoration.
All five states in the region have adopted voluntary targets to achieve land degradation neutrality (LDN) under UN Sustainable Development Goal 15.3.
For Tajikistan, where much of the territory consists of mountainous regions, land conservation becomes not only an environmental task but also a matter of food security and sustainable development of rural areas.

title: 烈士没留下照片，一群大学生却"画"出了他们的模样
content: 盛夏的皖中大地，骄阳似火。在安徽合肥，86岁的夏广英正在家中等待着一场迟到了82年的"见面"。 夏广英要"见"的人是她的父亲夏铁烈士。1944年，时任嘉山县洪山乡乡长的夏铁为掩护革命队伍突围，在战斗中牺牲，年仅34岁。彼时的夏广英只有4岁，战乱环境下，家中没有留存父亲照片，父亲的样貌仅依靠亲属口述想象，这成为老人长久的心结。 那天，当安徽师范大学（以下简称安徽师大）美术学院2023级学生李明玥携带着夏铁烈士画像来到夏广英家时，这位已经身患癌症的老人说"这辈子再也没有遗憾了"。 夏广英端详着父亲的画像。 李明玥是该校"红色青春守护人"志愿服务活动团队的成员，该团队的主要工作就是以素描复原烈士容貌，为烈士家属弥补未见亲人的遗憾。 "我终于见到你了" 李明玥画中的夏铁身着粗布短衫，兼具旧式教书先生的温和与革命者的坚毅。端详画像后，夏广英提出调整意见："家里长辈说，父亲的眉毛比较浓密，画像看着浅了些。" 李明玥当即取出绘画工具，对画像眉眼线条进行调整。修改完成后，夏广英反复抚摸画中人面部，低声说道："我永远不会忘记你，我的爸爸，我终于见到你了。" 那一刻，李明玥觉得，"我们是用画笔与时间赛跑，与不断消失的人和记忆赛跑。多画一张烈士画像，就能多促成一个家庭的重逢" 。 为完成这幅画像，她耗时一个半月，创作全程缺少烈士本人影像，只能参照烈属照片，剥离衰老特征，还原其30多岁时的样貌；军装、服饰、发型等细节逐一对照史料，多次将修改稿发给烈士家属，再根据反馈一遍遍调整。 "课本里的英烈大多只有文字评价，很难直观感受他们背后的家庭与人生。"李明玥说，创作过程中她始终担心细节偏差辜负老人的等待，"这不仅仅是一幅素描，更承载着一个女儿一生的等待与思念"。 烈士亲属一家和志愿者团队合影。 在安徽师大，李明玥并不是唯一一个给烈士画像的人。 据该校辅导员王伟介绍，"红色青春守护人"志愿服务活动于2021年启动。当年，王伟带领6名首批学生志愿者开展工作。目前，该团队已有400余名在校学生参与，累计完成对600余位烈士的容貌复原，志愿服务范围覆盖安徽、江西、浙江等地，并常态化前往烈士亲属住所、烈士陵园等地开展送画工作。 一支画笔的使命 王伟告诉《中国科学报》，为烈士画像并非单一的美术创作，而是一套包含史料考证、手绘创作、人工智能影像修复、实地走访、红色宣讲、绘本制作等在内的完整实践流程，学生全程参与各环节。 志愿者前往各地送画。 烈士画像的线索来源分为两类--由各地退役军人事务部门提供的烈士信息，以及一些烈属看到相关的公益事迹报道后主动联系。 "缺少烈士原始照片是普遍的难点。"2024年开始画像的该校学生潘宏宇对此深有体会。1943年春，新婚不久的河北青年王良参加解放军，并随着部队南下。妻子得知部队要经过隔壁村，便连夜缝制袜子送到丈夫手中，这也成了两人的永别。新中国成立后，妻子等来了一纸烈士证明书。此后，她再未改嫁。如今104岁的她想有一张与丈夫的结婚照。 了解到家属诉求后，潘宏宇花了一个多月，前后修改多版画像。他很清楚画像不能有一丝一毫的马虎，这既是对烈士的尊重，又是对烈属的负责。"表情严肃还是微笑？穿长衫还是短衫？戴的徽章什么样式......"他一边画一边思考。 最终，依据烈士弟弟的面部特征以及其遗孀的模糊记忆，潘宏宇绘制了夫妻二人的第一张新婚画像，完成了烈士妻子一辈子的心愿。 潘宏宇绘制的王良夫妻合照。 "我们现在20多岁，王良烈士牺牲时和我们差不多大。"潘宏宇说，"我们在学校安稳学习，他却奔赴战场再也没能回家。绘画过程中，我时常会想他当年作出抉择时的心境。" 作为项目启动时的6名首批志愿者之一，陈如意曾绘制过抗美援朝烈士王金生的画像。她告诉记者："校内人物写生时，我们面对的是模特，创作标准仅停留在造型准确层面。但绘制烈士画像时，除了要还原五官外形，还需要通过线条、神态体现革命者精神特质，绘画不再只是技巧练习。" 志愿者与烈属沟通画像细节。 交付画像只是实践的一环，团队依托美术专业拓展多项配套--组建10余人的红色宣讲团，先后走进部队、中小学、高校开展30余场爱国主义宣讲；成立绘本创作小组，完成《李家发革命故事绘本》《寻淮洲革命故事绘本》等12册红色绘本，印制5000册免费发放至乡村学校。 "铭记他们是我们的责任" 2022年，在为烈士画像项目启动一年后，王伟曾邀请青年志愿者分享画像经历，为新生上了一堂特别的入党启蒙教育课。那些烈士"回家"的故事在学生心中埋下一颗红色种子。每当群里发布"为烈士画像"活动通知，大家都抢着回复，手机很快便被一行行"我报名"刷屏。 "是因为有学分吗？"记者问。 王伟摇了摇头："活动没有学分、没有硬性考核要求，同学们都是发自内心地去做这件事情。" 2023年10月，为了给青年志愿者一个"家"，安徽师大专门成立了"红色青春守护人"工作室，由王伟担任负责人，并在学校大学生活动中心腾出一间画室。青年志愿者从此有了固定作画、交流和开展活动的场所。 工作室内，同学们正在画像。 短短5年时间，从6人志愿小组发展至400 余人常态化参与，为何如此多的学生都愿意参与其中？ "项目全程改变了教师单向布置任务的模式，将实践各环节主动权交给学生。"王伟说，"绘画中的各个环节都有学生参与。反复沟通打磨、线下送画、见证家属圆梦的经历，让学生产生成就感，觉得自己的画笔是有价值、有意义的，他们自然愿意参加。" 据王伟观察，长期以来，美术专业学生常常会被贴上"绘画脱离现实、专业价值有限"的标签。学生的作品仅限于课堂，难以让他们真正感受到美术的社会价值。而该项目将人像素描、插画设计、数字媒体、视觉设计等专业课程内容与红色实践巧妙结合，同步实现了学生专业能力提升与思想教育--课堂人像造型训练直接运用于烈士容貌复原；平面设计技能用于乡村红色文创、烈士陵园展板制作，插画能力用于红色绘本创作；数字方向学生负责人工智能彩色修复、红色主题短视频剪辑...... 此外，为了持续提升学生的获得感，"红色青春守护人"工作室还联合芜湖传媒中心推出了"小手拉大手"身边的榜样系列青春思政课，邀请志愿者分享志愿服务背后的故事，现已录制40余期节目。 安徽师大为"烈士画像"志愿服务宣讲会。 闻清晓是在一次讲座上听一位学姐分享她的志愿服务故事后，决定加入团队的。"我至今还记得那位学姐说：'为了和平，为了祖国，多少人再也看不到亲人的面孔，只剩下脑海中模糊的记忆。保家卫国是他们的使命，而铭记他们是我们的责任。'那一刻，我意识到我们的画笔是有用的，是可以让亲人跨越时空再次相聚的。"她说。 正是为了促成这份跨越时空的团聚，在安徽师大，这场跨越时空的青春对话仍在持续推进。
